REPOR T OF THE GRAND TREASURER

O•AMD MA.,...

OF CALIFORN IA
•AN P'RANCllCO

59

I am privileged to present to you my seventh Annual Report as your Grand
Treasurer. All of the financial data contained therein is based upon the official
audit statements of Lindquist, von Husen and Joyce, Certified Public Accountants for each of our four Masonic entities at June 30th, 1977.
Your Grand Treasurer attests that our accounting procedures, now and in the
past, have been on a modified cash basis, and all are in proper form and as stated
by the Certified Public Accountants; the financial statements present fairly the
assets, liabilities and fund balances of the transactions of the several entities.
Your Grand Treasurer is accountable for approximately 66 million dollars in
cash and securities at cost, as well as 17 million dollars in real estate and notes
receivable. The securities are safely deposited in the vaults of the Crocker Bank,
# 1 Montgomery Street, San Francisco.
Unannounced, on the 10th day of June this year, your Grand Treasurer,
together with the Assistant Grand Treasurer, Kem Copeland, and two members
of our accounting staff entered the vaults of the Crocker Bank and made a
physical check of our securities. All were verified, and the totals confirmed to be
in accord with our office records.
I would like to comment on each of our four Masonic entities:
The Grand Lodge itself indicates an excess of expense over income of
$86,689, less a gain of $61,270 on sale of securities, resulting in a net loss of
$25,419, which sum together with $9,540 for retirement of fixed assets reduces
our fund balance in the Grand Lodge account to $1,536,928. Likewise the
Brethren of the Grand Lodge should be informed that the marketable securities in
this account are valued at 71 % of cost. In the statement of appropriations the
Grand Master appfoved supplemental expenditures of $61,525 some of which are
non-recurring. In view of the above supplemental expenditures, I wish to
reiterate the statement made in my 1976 report that: "To the end that better
controls be provided in our financial affairs, your Grand Treasurer recommends
that no funds in excess of the budgeted amounts authorized by this Grand Lodge,
be paid out, unless approved by the Committee on Finance and/or authorized by
the Grand Master."
. The assets of the California Masonic Foundation continue in excess of one
million dollars. Value of securities at June 30, 1977 was 84% of cost. Income of
approximately $83,000 to the Foundation was expended in the main for leadership, health and educational grants.
The California Masonic Memorial Temple activities for the year ending June
30th, 1977 resulted in a loss of $137,262. Included in those figures is an item of
$166,463 for depreciation, which, if deducted from the operating loss, would
show a positive cash flow of approximately $29,000 compared to about $96,000
for last year. An increased expense of approximately $63,000 was due to
waterproofing all concrete walls, cleaning all exterior marble, treating and
painting all exterior metal surfaces and the replacement of a sidewalk. This major
non-recurring expense together with the sum of $15,000 for a feasibility study
accounted for the major part of the reduction in cash flow.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipfal Grand lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
My services as your Grand Secretary commenced at the close of Annual
Communication in 1960, and this is my seventeenth Annual Report to Grand
Lodge. The Office of Grand Secretary includes, as part of its responsibilities,
duties as Secretary for the Masonic Homes of California, California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the California Masonic Foundation, the California Masonic
Retirement Plan, the Investment Committee, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund
and other Committees of Grand Lodge.
All financial records and supporting papers, vouchers and books for each of
the entities are on file in the Grand Lodge office. Your Grand Lodge Staff
maintains the records pertaining to the various entities mentioned above.
The Finance Committee and its Chairman, as required by Masonic law, have
reviewed details of the disbursement made by Grand Lodge during the year.
There is recorded in the Grand Treasurer's Report all monies received and
credited to the accounts under his name and custody as provided by law.
UNFINISHED BUSINESS

The following matters were continued from the Communication of l fJ76:
I. Master Mason Proficiency, 3rd Degree (1976 Proceedings, page 229).
2. Physical Qualification for Degrees (1976 Proceedings, page 251).
3. Study Use of Holy Writings other than Holy Bible ( 1976 Proceedings, page
31).
4. Veteran Award Ceremony, Evaluation (1976 Proceedings, page 85).
Also, there is a matter of unfinished business from the Communication of
1975:
Permit Youth Groups to Solicit Public (1976 Proceedings, page 201).

LISTING OF INVF.sTMENTS
As noted in my 'report last year, for many years there was reproduced in the
Grand Treasurer's Report and the Annual Proceedings a det~led listing of
investments. The list was substantial but was out of date by the time it appeared
in printed form. We maintain a continuing inventory of all investments on
computer. Details, therefore, are not printed in the Annual Proceedings, but any
member of Grand Lodge may review the copies of our investment portfolio in the
Grand Secretary's Office.

GRAND LOOOE OFFICE
With Grand Lodge approval last year for the appropriate capital expenditures
your Grand Lodge Office has been remodelled. This is the first major renovation
which has been made. Walls have been moved, partitions changed and lighting
improved. An acoustical tile ceiling and carpeting throughout the office were
installed as an aid to soundproofing. Also, we now have an adequate employees'
lunch room on the office floor. We are confident that the members of Grand
Lodge will be proud of the results. Employees have woJk facilities which are
more conducive to effective production. Each of you is invited to visit the Office
and observe the new facilities .

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence has reviewed the applications for dispensations acted upon by the Grand Master and his approval of Life Membership
Resolutions and find that he has acted properly in granting or denying dispensations and in approving Life Membership .Resolutions, except in two instances.
The request of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 to receive and act upon the
application of a rejected Candidate failed to show that due notice of the meeting,
at which the ballot for application for dispensation was to be taken, was given to
each of its members.
The request of Artesia Lodge No. 377 to receive and act upon the application
of a rejected Candidate failed to show that due notice of the meeting, at which the
ballot for application for dispensation was to be taken, was given to each of its
members, and also failed to show that the ballot vote was unanimous.
The Committee once again calls to the attention of Lodge Secretaries that
many of the applications for dispensation to hold an election other than the stated
time failed to certify that the requesting Lodge had complied with the requirements of Section 2502 of the California Masonic Code, particularly the requirements that two-thirds of the members present at a Stated Meeting voted to request
a dispensation and setting forth specifically the reasons for the request.
We recommend that, except for the two instances, the actions of the Grand
Master be approved, and that in the cases of Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 and
Artesia Lodge No. 377, the Lodge be requested to furnish proper certification.
Respectfully submitted,
LEO E. ANDERSON, Chairman

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on By-Laws:
The Grand Lodge Committee on By-Laws held their annual meeting on
Mond~y, October IO, 1977, and reviewed the numerous proposed amendments
to therr Lodge By-Laws as initiated by many of the constituent Lodges of this
Jurisdiction.
Some 134 changes to Lodge By-Laws were submitted during the Masonic year
by I 14 Lodges, and these changes were examined by this Committee to ascertain
that the changes were in compliance with the California Masonic Code and the
Uniform Code of By-Laws.
As a result of .the Committee's review, it was found that the proposed
amendments were m order with the following exceptions:
A. The request by EI Camino Research Lodge to change its By-Laws in
respect to the counties wherein special meetings of the Lodge may be held

74

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

appears to contain a typographical error. It appears that the referen~e to an
amendment of Section 2 of Article III should have properly read Section 3 of
Article III.
B. The initial request by Crocker Lodge No. 454 to change the date of its
Stated Meeting as a result of a fire which seriously damaged its Temple, was
technically in error because the amendment was not adopted on a regular
Stated Meeting night; however, this error became moot when the By-Laws
were again amended to return the meeting night to the original first Tuesday of
each month. It is to be noted, however, that an error still exists in that while
the By-Laws now provide that said first Tuesday shall not apply "when the
regular meeting date shall fall on New Year's or Independence Day, legal
holidays, or during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge" the language
of the Uniform Code of By-Laws is not followed to provide for an alternate
date for such Stated Meetings.
C. In the requests of Ophir Lodge No. 33 for an increase in its fees and for
an increase in its dues, it is noted that the Lodge Seal has not been affixed to
the Certification as required by Section 2076 of the California Masonic Code.
D. Again it is noted that the Lodge Seal has been omitted from the
Certifications in respect to proposed changes in Lodge meeting places by
Molino Lodge No. 150, Utopia Lodge No. 537, Composite Lodge No. 639,
San Antonio Lodge No. 694, San Juan Lodge No. 732, Highland Lodge No.
748, Moreno Valley Lodge No. 804, and William B. Ogden Lodge No. 816.
A reference to Section 2076 referred to above discloses the requirement that:
"all documents .... emanating from such Lodge, or from its Master or
Secretary in his official capacity, shall bear the impress of such seal or be
considered null and of no effect.''
It is suggested that the form furnished by the office of the Grand Secretary for
these changes be modified so as to call the attention of the Lodges to the
requirement that the seal be affixed.
E. The request of Arcata Lodge No. 106 does not fully conform to Section
2086 of the California Masonic Code (Uniform Code of By-Laws) in that it
fails to permit payment of dues quarterly in advance. ·
.
F. Roseville Lodge No. 222, in its request to increase its dues, has failed to
comply with the requirements of Section 1 of Article XIII of the Uniform Code
of By-Laws (Section 2086, CMC) in that the amendment was not adopted at
the next Stated Meeting following its introduction. This resolution should be
reintroduced and readopted to correct this error.
F. The request of Alpha Lodge No. 431, for an increase in its dues, again
lacks the Lodge Seal on the Certification by the Secretary.
G. Of a minor nature are the attempts by Ashlar Lodge No. 306 and West
Gate Lodge No. 335 in their amendments dealing with increases in dues to
include a commencement date for said increase. These effective dates should
not be a part of the By-Law language but should properly be covered by a
separate provision in the resolution establishing such an effective date.
H. The certificates of Atwater Lodge No. 622, Livingston Lodge No. 658,
and Lakeside Lodge No. 760 for increases in their dues should be reprepared

Your committee, in response to the instructions of Grand Lodge given at the
1976 Communication, and in cooperation with the Grand Secretary, has made a
survey of those Lodges which have continued to operate on the $12 minimum
d~es. Responses were received from 18 to 21 Lodges involved. This survey
disclosed that although one of these Lodges has, this current year, found it
necessary to increase its dues, the 20 remaining Lodges are able to maintain
themselves with minimum dues.
An analysis of the numerous increases seems to disclose also that the need for
additional monies is more inclined to arise in the larger m~tro~litan areas where
real estate taxes on existing temples are ever on the rise.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is the opinion of this Committee, therefore, concurred in by the Grand
Secretary, that our present legislation in respect to minimum dues and in respect
to amendments to Lodge By-Laws to permit dues increases is adequate and
although the matter should be reviewed periodically, no present changes appear
necessary in this regard.
The Grand Secretary and his staff have, as always, provided efficient and
diligent assistance to both the constituent Lodges and to this Committee. We
extend our gratitude to Brother Siems and his associates for their help which has
greatly simplified our work, and we encourage Lodges contemplating changes to
their By-Laws to take advantage of this dedicated and knowledgeable group of
people by securing from them the necessary forms and instructions to accomplish
the desired changes. They can make your work much simpler.
Respectfully submitted,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Your Committee has carefully examined the Petitions for Restoration of L. I.
N. in Trial Record No. 1919 from William B. Ogden Lodge No. 816 and
Harding Lodge No. 584; and W. B. S. in Trial Record No. 2066, from Long
Beach Lodge No. 327; and found that in each case the actions of the accused
were contrary to the tenets of Masonry and that there has been an insufficient
showing that the applicant is worthy and that his standing and character are s~ch
as to entitle him to be restored to membership. We therefore offer the following
resolution:
RESOLVED that the Petition for restoration in Trial Records No. 1919 and
2066 be denied without prejudice.

The findings of fact by the commissioners on the two precise specifications
were on conflicting evidence. One specification charged the accused with
actually furnis~ing the .fi~ms ~d a projector and the other specification charged
the. accused with providing his home on another occasion for a stag party at
which pornographic films were shown to DeMolays and at which liquor was
served to DeMolays. While the Trial Review Committee cannot set aside the
find~gs ~f the comm~ssioners that the accused was not guilty of the precise
specifications set forth m the original charge, it is clear from the evidence that the
accused failed in his duties as a Mason and is guilty of un-Masonic conduct.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that this Grand Lodge affirm the findings by the commissioners
on the original charge; but that this Grand Lodge direct the Junior Warden of
Yorba Linda Lodge No. 469 to charge the accused with a violation of Masonic
law . by. reason of his fai!ure to make any effective attempt to prevent the
furmshmg of poronograph1c films to a sixteen year old member of the Order of
DeMolay for the purpose of showing them to other minor young men and by
reason of his ~owingly facilitating the furnishing of such films for such purpose,
and that the trial on such charge or charges be in a Lodge to be designated by the
Grand Master.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2098

The accused, a member in good standing of Oildale Lodge. No. 688, i:v~s
charged with un-Masonic conduct in that he did, on or about May 5, 1976, sohc1t
another to commit and join in the crime of assault with a deadly weapon and
thereafter did attempt to set fire and burn a residential dwelling in violation of the
Penal Code of the State of California. Trial was held in the Superior Court of
Kern County wherein the accused was convicted of both felony counts and was
sentenced by the Court.
A Masonic trial was convened in Oildale Lodge early this year, at which time
the accused changed his plea to guilty.
The Trial Master set his penalty at suspension.
The Trial Review Committee read and evaluated the State Court proceeding,
the transcripts, including the accused's own statements, and conclude his
defenses are insufficient to exculpate him from the effect of his demonstrated
intent to violate his Masonic obligations. We believe his actions were so alien to
our principles that the penalty should be raised to expulsion.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the accused plea of guilty be accepted, the findings of the
Trial Master be accepted, but that the penalty be raised to expulsion.
TRIAL RECORD No. 2102

The trial transcript in this case, including the accused's own statements,
contains uncontroverted evidence that, although he could have done so, the
accused failed to make an effective attempt to prevent or to discourage the
furnishings of three pornographic films to a sixteen year old member of the Order
of DeMolay for the purpose of showing them to other minor young men. The
evidence shows that the accused was a DeMolay advisor who knew of the plan to
furnish such pornographic films to the DeMolay and of the DeMolay's intention
to show them to other minor young men. By his own testimony the accused
claimed that one of the accused's employees was to furnish such films. It is
uncontroverted also that the accused knowingly facilitated the furnishing of such
films by his employee and the picking up of the films at the accused's home by
the DeMolay for the purpose of showing them to his football team. Th~ ac~used' s
explanations fall short of excusing him in any way for his acts and his failure to
act.

79

TRIAL RECORD No. 2106

This trial involved a member of Capital City Lodge No. 499, F. & A. M. in
Sacramento who for 21 years had been employed by the Sacramento Municipal
Utility District as a lineman and troubleshooter.
By his own admission, greed was his undoing. He sought to supplement his
$22,000 per year inc9me by helping himself to certain of the District's material
and tools, including but not limited to, copper wiring, silver strips, magnetic
starter motors and miscellaneous personal property. This material which was
worth in excess of $5,000.00 was subsequently converted into cash by selling it
t~ scrap letal d~lers. to supplement his $22,000 per year income by helping
h1m~elf to certain of the District's material and tools, including but not and
receive not more than 3 years' probation. He was found guilty as charged.
1:he .sen~ence was fixed at 300 hours of volunteer service; 3 years probation;
restitution m the amount of $5,199.93; payment of a $1000 fine and 90 days in
the county jail. The jail time was stayed for 6 months and the record does not
disclose whether the accused actually served time in jail.
The Trial Committee found the accused guilty of un-Masonic conduct and
fixed the penalty at suspension.
Because of the seriousness of the crime and to achieve uniformity of punishment throughout the Jurisdiction, your Committee on Trial Review believes the
sentence should be raised to expulsion.
We therefore submit the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilt in Trial Record No. 2106 be approved
but that the penalty be raised to expulsion and the member be expelled from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

TRIAL RECORD 2107
An Entered Apprentice Mason in Los Gatos Lodge No. 292 was charg~d with
three specifications of un-Masonic conduct essentiall~ involving the lending of a
considerable sum of monies to the Entered Apprentice Mason by a member of
Los Gatos Lodge for the purpose of starting a business venture. Both individu_als
were represented by independent counsel, each ?f whon_i d~med the transaction
to be of a highly speculative nature and so advised their clients.
Regretfully, the business venture failed, ultimately requiring the Entered
Apprentice and his wife to file petitions in Bankruptcy and each ~as subsequently discharged by the Bankruptcy Court from the payment of all hsted debts
without objection by the accuser.
.
While there were numerous errors at the Masonic trial of the accused which
perhaps would justify reversal of the conviction of the accused, your. Committee
is more concerned that the charges should ever have been entertained by the
Worshipful Master.
Section 33 l 2(b) of the California Masonic Code clearly provides: '' Inabil~ty to
pay a just debt as promised, because of financial difficulties, no moral turpitude
being involved, is not a Masonic offense."
.
Your committee finds no moral turpitude involved in the subject charges.
While we are extremely sympathetic with the parties who lose consider~le
sums in business ventures, a Masonic Lodge is not a proper tribunal before which
members may or should seek to enforce payment of debts or to try their honest
business disputes.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED that in Trial Record 2107 the findings of the trial commission
shall be reversed, that the charges be dismissed and the accused be restored to his
proper status as an Entered Apprentice Mason.
By separate actions each of the resolutions were Adopted.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Time moves relentlessly on, and once again the hour for accounting is at hand.
Among the many duties of the Grand Lecturer is that of rendering to the Grand
Lodge at each annual communication; a report of the condition of the Lodges
within the California Jurisdiction, together with a detailed account of his services
throughout the year.
In compliance with those requirements, the following report is most respectfully offered:
Some abbreviation of this report was necessary due to the many and varied
activities of the past year, but none of the essentials were deleted.
"Masonry on the Move" is the name-M asonic activity is the game! Under
the very able leadership of Grand Master Kermit A. Jacobson, many new areas of
activity have been initiated in the various Lodges. This new activity could very
well signal the end of declining membership in California Masonry, and a return
to healthy, growing Lodges. Much more work needs to be done however, and
complacency could destroy all of the valuable gains which have been made this
year.
The Ritual Committee has been pleased to work in close cooperation with the
Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Information and Responsibility this year.
All day seminars have been held in various locations within the six divisions. At
these seminars, the morning has been given to instruction in the ritual, and the
afternoon to matters of Masonic information and administration.
These all day seminars have been very enthusiastically received by all the
Brethren, and it is the consensus of opinion that the purposes of Masonry are
being well served in these informative and useful work sessions. A total of 9
were held last yeas- more are planned for next year. You are all urged to attend
these seminars whenever they occur within your area.
Evidence of increased activity within the Lodges is found in the annual reports
of the Inspectors. Among the questions which the Inspectors are required to
answer in the annual report form is, "Do the Lodges carry on a significant
program of activities to interest the membership?" - "Are Lodges having
difficulty in securing new officer material?" - "Are the Lodges of your District
filling the needs of their communities?" and, "Is Masonry advancing in your
district?"
Some very interesting facts emerge from the answers to these questions,
particularly when this information is compared to that which was received in
reports of former years.
The Inspectors' reports of July l, 1976 indicated that 95 percent of all
California Lodges were then carrying on significant programs of activity to
interest the members hip-that only 46 percent of all Lodges were reporting
difficulty in securing new officer material?"__:" Are the Lodges of your District
then filling the needs of their communities, and that Masonry was advancing in
92 percent of all California Lodges. In comparison, the Inspectors' reports of
July 1, 1977 produce the following information:
96.5 percent of the Inspectors report that the Lodges within their Districts are
now carrying on significant programs of activity to interest the membership, an

You have become a part of a very elite Corps, Brethren, and we proudly offer
you our complete support in your new duties.
It is noted with deep pride that Lodge contributions to the California Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund for 1977 are in excess of one million dollars. The three
principal tenets of Masonry could be no more beautifully exemplified than in
this spontaneous outpouring of Brotherly concern for the welfare of those unable
to do for themselves. "No greater love hath any man."
The Inspectors' reports indicate that all but a few of the Lodges have performed
well in the area of required Grand Lodge programs for the year. The fact that a
total of 38 Cornerstone Ceremonies were conducted this year as an indication that
the Lodges have carried on very active programs-Public Schools and Constitution Observance programs have been exceptionally well performed, and more
than 200 other Grand Lodge programs such as receptions, dedications, anniversary celebrations and other ceremonies have been carried out throughout the
Jurisdiction. The "Hiram Award" program which has been conducted in Galt,
and in Palisades Lodge have commanded extremely high interest among members and friends. I was quite pleased to serve as Master of Ceremonies for the
Constitution Observance Program which was sponsored by Officers and members of three Masonic Districts in Division Five just two weeks ago. This
program which was held in the Municipal Auditorium of the City of Glendale
included a musical presentation of a group of young girls from 9 to 16 called the
"Songsmiths." It also included a wonderful address by the famous newscaster,
George Putnam, and the presentation to him of the first Masonic Americanism
A ward. Programs of this type are a valuable weapon for the Lodges in their fight
to regain the interest of members, and a great deal of credit is due those Officers
and Brothers who have expended a great deal of time and effort in getting these
programs off the ground. In Galt it was Senior Warden Walter F. Heimgartner,
who turned out a• crowd of 400 for a crab feed in a Lodge whose total
membership is only 104, and to the Senior Warden of America Lodge in Los
Angeles, Burt Bronson, assisted greatly by Inspector Phil Hylton. These
Brothers would not take "no" for an answer, and they did what everyone told
them could not be done. Senior Warden Burt Bronson, expended so much of his
energy in arranging the Glendale program that he suffered a mild heart attack the
night before the performance and didn't even get to see the fruits of his labors.
He has recovered sufficiently ·to enable him to be here in this auditorium today.
It is evident from the reports of the Inspectors that satisfactory levels of
activity are being maintained in most of the Lodges. Those few Lodges which are
not now carrying on such programs, but desire to do so, may receive assistance
from the wonderful new Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Resources which is
chaired by Worshipful Everett Houser. In its first year, this Committee has
assisted a score of failing Lodges to overcome some seemingly insurmountable
obstacles. The services of this specialized Committee are available to· any Lodge
which has problems of a nature which seem to defy solution.
HA WADAN MASONRY

Two years ago it was agreed that the Laymans' Night Program should be
instituted in Hawaii. Worshipful Jesse Kelly, Master of Hawaiian Lodge No. 21,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

volunteered to become the main speaker and conduct the program in the various
Island Lodges. Unfortunately, just before Brother Kelly was to start the program,
he suffered a fatal heart attack, thereby forcing the abandonment of plans for
Laymans' Night in the Islands. Being thoroughly convinced of the value of this
program, I determined to carry on for Brother Jesse Kelly . Dates were established for Laymans' Nights in the ten Hawaiian Lodges, and I accompanied
Assistant Grand Lecturer Ulysses G. Patropulos to Honolulu in late May to start
the program. In the following two weeks we held Laymans' nights and Ritual
Schools in each of the ten Hawaiian Lodges, with the result that the light of
understanding was brought to our Hawaiian Brethren, and at least 14 good
qualified men of the Islands sought admission into the Lodges of the area. The
effort expended in this regard was more than justified, and it is my sincere hope
that this valuable and productive program will be perpetuated in the Lodges of
Hawaii. The tenets of Freemasonry continue to shine brightly among the
Brethren of Hawaii, and friendship abounds. Masonry is "on the move" in the
Island State.
My deep appreciation is extended to the three Island Inspectors-W illiam
McKee, Ozzie Lau and Bruce Barnes, together with the wonderful Masters,
Wardens and Brethren of the IO Hawaiian Lodges for all their assistance, and for
teaching this Grand Lecturer what brotherly love really means .

And finally, my Brethren, I thank you-for your support and understanding,
and for your encouragement which has come to me through your notes, letters
and calls.
My thoughts and actions this past year have all been directed toward the
betterment of Masonry by sharing of Masonic information, education of new
Masons and old Officers, attempting the elimination of intolerance within the
Fraternity, ~d by supporting the concept of "Masonry on the Move."
Those act10ns are now commended to your consideration. Thank you my
Brethren .

l'J'77-78 BUDGET
Every member of the Ritual Team has struggled valiantly this year to maintain
the expense of teaching ritual at the lowest level. Our success in this regard is
attested to in the fact that our total expenditures last year were well within our
projected budget. Inflation and rising costs of accommodations make it necessary
to increase our estimates of cost for next year. We have reluctantly adjusted our
budget request upward to offset these increased costs of ritual instruction, and we
request that the amount of $53,500.00 be approved for the Ritual Committee
Budget for 1977-78.

duties this year have established new standards of excellence. I extend sincerest
gratitude to Most Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson, a truly great Grand Master
whose actions this year have brought new luster to the office. The inspired
leadership of this marvelous Mason has brought California Masonry many new
programs which will benefit every member of Masonry in California for many
years to come. For all that he has taught me, not the least of which is patience in
times of stress, I thank him from the bottom of my heart.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES OF THE
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M. of California:
Although we may recite by rote that to relieve the distressed is a duty
incumbent on all men, but particularly on Masons, we nevertheless know that
without adherence to this great tenet, Masonry would be materially encumbered
in its mission.
It is in reaffirmation of this spirit that the Board of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California respectfully presents the eighty-fifth report on its stewardship to the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge for the fiscal year July l, 1976,
through June 30, 1977.
ORGANIZATION OF THE BOARD

The responsibility for the operations of the Masonic Homes of California has
been entrusted by Grand Lodge to the Board of Trustees . The Board numbers
twelve, including the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens who serve by virtue of their offices. Also, the Grand Treasurer and the
Grand Secretary serve as treasurer and secretary of the Board.
Nine of the trustees of the Board are appointed and come from divers areas of
California. Appointive trustees may serve only three successive three-year terms.
As of June 30, 1977, the Board included the following trustees, appointed by the
Grand Master for terms expiring as of the close of the Annual Communication of
Grand Lodge in the years indicated.

ORGANIZATION OF STAFF

Executive administration of the Homes is provided by Raymond A. Howe
(346), a former trustee and retired business manager of the Palo Alto Medical
Clinic. Brother Howe is charged with the responsibility of carrying out the
policies promulgated by the Board. His experience and dedication have been
valuable assets to the direction of the Homes and especially during the building
rehabilitation program at Decoto.
J. Burton Brown (334) has completed his first full year as Administrator of the
Masonic Home at Decoto. He has demonstrated an especial talent in relating to
the needs of the residents and in creating as near a home atmosphere as is
possible in group living conditions.
James C. Blaine (104) has completed his eleventh year as Administrator of the
Home for Children at Covina. He continues to execute the Home program in such
a way as to simulate a cluster of young families living and working together, thus
replacing the family life these young people have lost.
Field investigators, Sue Collins (Northern California) and Martha Quick
(Southern California), provide a continuing service in meeting the needs of
applicants, their families, and Lodge representatives. Their responsibilities
include personal interviews, preparing written reports for the Board, contacting
social service agencies, and assisting in every way in the transition from their
former life, to residence in the Home. During the construction rehabilitation
period at Decoto, they are keeping in constant touch with those approved for
admission but waiting for the actual move into the Home, lending assistance
whenever and wherever needed.
OPERATIONS

Trustees meet monthly, alternating between the North and South including
meetings at the Homes at Decoto and Covina. Various committees of the Board
meet separately on such· matters as scholarship allocations, major maintenance
programs, real estate transactions, budgetary control, and the rehabilitation work
now in progress at Decoto.

Any program which calls for the expenditure of more than twelve million
dollars deserves the continuing attention of Grand Lodge, even though the
planning and implementation have been ongoing for the past three years.
First in importance was the completion of the "life safety" system for Decoto
which included an upgrading of the buildings to code requirements and a
comprehensive seismic study to determine the location of earthquake faults and
to analyze the structural integrity of the present buildings. The water distribution
system was renovated and a fire hydrant system installed around the property.
Fire doors and smoke detectors were installed. The building used for dining and
assembly was found to be unsafe for occupancy and was demolished. New
medical equipment and furnishings were purchased for the skilled nursing facility
and the medical staff was increased.
In the second phase attention was given to the comfort and enjoyment of the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

residential guests with a painting and decorating program which included new
carpeting and drapes.

.
We are now entering the third and final stage of the rehabihtatJon plan which
calls for the remodeling of each of the residential rooms with individual showers,
toilets, and wash basins. By early 1979 a new Central Services Building will
have been completed, providing dining and kitchen facilities, recreation rooms,
and a mall containing a post office, coffee shop, beauty shop, and other
amenities.
The responsibility for the planning and execution of the renovation of Dc:coto
has rested primarily with the Rehabilitation Committee under the leadership of
Trustee Charles H. Sedam. Paramount in the considerations of the Committee
has been the safety, comfort, and morale of the residents of Decato, and whi~e
the cost seems high even in terms of today's inflated dollars, the end result .is
considered to be worth it as this will be one of the finest homes for the elderly in
the country.

fact that the cost of operating and maintaining the Homes at Decato and Covina,
of general and administrative expenses, and outside relief during the past fiscal
year amounted to $4,259,861. What a compliment it is to the Masons of
California that this cost was completely funded with the help of an annual per
capita assessment of only $1.00. Since it is our belief that without government
subsidy or welfare assistance Masons truly take care of their own, the Board
recommends that the allocation of $1.00 per member be continued during the
ensuing year.

PROPERTY STUDY
The trustees are giving serious study to the best use of the 267 acres w~ich now
comprise the Masonic Homes property at Union City. It has been determined that
annexation to the city of Union City would be of beneficial interest and the Board
has voted to support such an action.
The Masonic Home now occupies for its operations 50 acres of the to~ 267
acres. There are approximately 29 acres fronting on Mission Boulevard, situated
on both sides of the entrance to the Home, for which a substantial offer has been
made. Although the offer has not been accepted, the Board will continue its study
and investigation to determine ~he feasibility of selling a portion of this frontage
acreage as surplus property.
FINANCIAL
Because of the continuing generosity and the constant concern for the Masonic
Homes long displayed by the Masons of California, the inco~e ~om the Hom~s
Endowment Fund is providing the mainstay source of operating income .. Agam
this year, the Endowment Board under the Chairmanship of Robert E. H~lts has
exceeded the one million dollar mark in contributions. As a result, the mcome
from the Endowment Fund investments coupled with those of the Homes Reserve
Fund provided nearly $3,600,000, or 84% of the total operating costs of the
Homes.
It is intended that the Homes reserves, at present fully invested, will provide
the funds to finance the cost of the rehabilitation program at Decato. It is
obvious however that the drain on such invested reserves will materially reduce
future ~ngs ~d their contribution toward operational expenses. But if the
past is any prolouge to the future, then the Trustees have. every con.fidenc~ that
the Masons of California through gifts and bequests and direct donations will, as
they have in the past, put forth every effort to replace the funds expended on the
rehabilitation program.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

To these graduates we wish good luck, and Godspeed as they enter into
another exciting chapter of their lives. Some will enter the labor market, others
will pursue higher education, some will enter the armed forces-all will
remember their years with us.
Many alumni have been aided by the Home in seeking further schooling to
prepare them for their life's work. This year, 1976-77, was no exception. Alumni
receiving scholarship aid included:

plus, many, many "drop in" contacts by our Brethren including Grand Lodge
Officers, Committeemen and Sojourners. We welcome them and extend the
invitation to our "larger family" to come see us!
Alumni Day was held May 22, 1977. Over 250 alumni came, ate, reminisced
and made plans for next year. A highlight of the day and evening was comparing
old snapshots of days gone by with color films made of alumni by "retired"
Brother Tom Hunter (1917-1919) whose hobby is traveling the United States,
contacting and filming every alumnus he can find. Brother Tom has an extensive
film library of lifelong Masonic Home friends.
Another alumnus, Brother Les Robert Davis ('37-'42), East San Diego Lodge
#561, still maintains close contact with our Home. He has been helpful in many
ways-both as an alumnus and as an attorney. "Brothers Tom and Les" are two
examples of male alumni who, after getting established, have joined our beloved
Craft. A random sampling, taken by your Administrator, these past 12 years, has
shown that 80% of our male alumni, have become Brothers. Masonry is
important, and relevant in the lives of the children served by the Fraternity.
We thank the Masons and concordant bodies in California and Hawaii for the
continuing support, love and dedication shown the children in our care. God
bless you all!

Several of these alumni have applied for continuing aid for next year, and
other alumni are in process of applying.
Our current population consists of 26 girls and 27 boys-total 53. Their ages
range from 6 to 17. We have 15 elementary school students, 16 Jr. High
students, and 22 high schoolers. Our children are involved in all school activities
including music, drama, gymnastics and all other sports. An extremely fine
relationship is maintained with the individual schools, the Charter Oak School
District and our local P.T.A.'s.
We have had a relatively healthy year with only two short hospitalizations. In
addition to annual physical and dental appointments, emergency treatment is
available by Magan Clinic and our very able nurse, Mrs. Ruby Thacker. Large
amounts of T.L.C. are available for our children daily and the price is right!
In addition to food, shelter, education, and good health, our children are
involved in a diverse and constructive leisure time activities program. Cultural
trips, concerts, athletics, arts, crafts, camping and beach trips are but a few
activities available. Contact is maintained with sponsoring Lodges as well as
participation in activities such as DeMolay, Job's Daughters and Rainbow. Our
Masonic concordant bodies supply us with invitations and tickets to B.B.Q's,
sporting events, circuses and other activities such as Disneyland, Magic Mountain, etc. For these acts of love, dedication and concern we are truly grateful.
Interest in our Covina Home has also been shown through our visitation
program. This past year, we have hosted picnics, tours, and "come and see"
events for:
38 Masonic Lodges and Districts
5 Hi-12 Clubs
11 Order of Eastern Star Chapters and Grand Officers
12 DeMolay Chapters and Advisory Councils
16 Job's Daughter Bethels and Guardians
14 Rainbow Assemblies, Districts and Advisors
47 "other" concordant groups

Respectfully submitted,
JAMES C. BLAINE, Administrator

Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board submits its 45th Annual Report

covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1977. We exceeded the million dollar
mark for the 5th straight year. This is the highest year yet!!!

Homes.

CONCLUSION

We extend a "Special Thanks" to our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful
Kermit A. Jacobson, for his leadership and for bringing the message to our
members throughout the Jurisdiction.
Our thanks to the Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, Inspectors,
Grand Lodge Committeemen, all of whom have supported this program, and to
the Masters and Wardens of the Lodges for their efforts in furthering this worthy
program with the members of their Lodges.
We are most grateful to the 100,917 Brethren who contributed $1,067,208.08
to the Permanent Endowment Fund.
The successful year we have just completed is an expression of love and
understanding by the Brethren of this Grand Lodge to the residents of our two
Homes. My thanks to the members of this Board for their dedicated effort in
making this an outstanding year.
Respectfully Submitted

144

, PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS

TAXES

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus takes pride in delivering the 50th
Annual Report of its activities covering the fiscal year July 1, 1976 through June
30, 1977.
Our Committee was formerly known as the Board of Control, and the name
was changed when the new California Masonic Code was published and released
recently.
The nineteen Masonic Service Bureaus in this Jurisdiction serve the sojourners and their widows and orphans while visiting or residing in the area served by
the Bureau.
The Right Worshipful Donald B. McCaw, Deputy Grand Master was appointed Liaison Officer to the Committee by the Grand Master. We appreciate
his assistance, and the cooperation and advice he gave during the past year.
NEW COMMITTEE MEMBERS

We welcome Worshipful Howard S. Fisher and Wilbur B. Taylor as two new
members of our Committee. Brother Fisher served on the Committee prior to his
appointment as Junior Grand Deacon in 1972 by the Most Worshipful William
H. Price. Worshipful Brother Taylor was appointed following the death of D.
Ewing Marsh in October 1976.
CORRESPONDENCE

Copies of important correspondence to and from the Committee was sent to the
Deputy Grand Master and each member of the Committee. The minutes of the
Committee Meetings were sent to the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, the
Grand Wardens and the Grand Secretary as well as the members of the
CoIRJDittee.
MEETINGS

The Committee held four meetings during the year. One meeting was held
during Grand Lodge Week in 1976 at which time we met with various Officers of
the Lodges who had questions about the operation of Masonic Service Bureaus.
We also handled routine business during the meeting.
One meeting was held in June 1977 to review the proposed Budgets for the
nineteen Bureaus.
A meeting was held early in February 1977 in Northern California which
included the Officers of the nine Bureaus located in that part of the State. There
were nineteen in attendance. One group meeting was held early in March in
Southern California which included the Officers of the ten Bureaus located in that
part of the State . There were twenty-five in attendance. During the group
meetings, a two-way communication is encouraged. These meetings have proven
valuable particularly to the new President of the Bureau and his Officers.

145

Continued attention has been directed to the importance of preparing both
Federal and State tax forms. The Committee has worked closely with Worshipful
W. Stanley Davis, Chairman of the Taxation Committee, and we are most
grateful for his services and advice.

BLOOD BANKS

Twelve of our Bureaus administer Blood Banks for their member Lodges and
others. A recent law was passed in California which prohibits the use of blood
from paid donors. This new law should have a minimum effect on the Blood
Banks administered by our Bureaus as nearly all the blood is donated by
volunteers.

as set forth.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
FILM AND CREATIVE PROJECTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Most Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson appointed the following Past Masters
and Worshipful Master to serve on this committee during the current Masonic
year: Walter L. Kemmerer (332), Victor T. Carbone (281), Jerry Rosen (415),
Thomas J. McKimson (602), Royal Dano (637), Sydney Zaid (415), Phil Gray

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

149

(415), Richard W. Sharpe (509); and reappointed William L. Funk (650), and
Donald G. Ingalls (542), Chairman.
Three meetings were held to plan and coordinate projects unique to the
function of this Committee.
Project 1: To institute and host a Jurisdictional-wide Annual Awards Night
designed to honor a Mason of outstanding character and extraordinary achievement reflecting the influence of Masonic ideals. There will be awards in two
categories: one to a living Mason and a posthumous award to an outstanding
Mason of the past. Rules of selection and criteria of achievement will be
determined by the Committee with the final selection of honorees to be made
each year by the Grand Master. The first awards program is scheduled to be held
in March of 1978 in the Los Angeles area. The coordinating unit consists of
Sydney Zaid, Jerry Rosen, Victor Carbone, Walter Kemmerer, and Donald
Ingalls.
Project II: The "Hiram Award" program was launched in February of this
year at Galt Lodge No. 267 in the community of Galt. This pilot program,
designed for use by Constituent Lodges, honored Past Master Glenn W. Ingram
of Galt Lodge in recognition of his outstanding service to his Lodge, the
community, and to Masonry in general. More than 400 persons, many of them
non-Masons, attended a Crab Feast held in Brother Ingram's honor. The program
proved to be an outstanding way for Lodges to give much needed recognition to
one of their own and a wonderful opportunity to bring Masonic activity to the
attention of the community at large. Hiram Award programs are now being
planned at other Lodges, and Galt Lodge is planning its second Hiram Award
Night for next year. Walter Kemmerer heads the coordinating unit and stands
ready to assist other Lodges interested in holding their own programs. Inquiries
are requested.
Project III: The design of special brochures was undertaken at the request of
the Grand Master. Work is being done on new concepts for the Youth Committee
and in the areas of Wills and Bequests and Special Gifts for the Masonic Homes,
as well as for the contemplated California Masonic Leaming Center. Thomas
McKimson is coordinator in this area.
Project IV: A financial study requested by the Grand Master to determine the
feasibility of producing a professional quality 16 mm film depicting the Masonic
Cornerstone Ceremony was completed, and a budget of 8,000 dollars for this
purpose was submitted in August to the Finance Committee. This sum represents
approximately one third of the total cost, the balance to be provided through
outside service at no cost to Grand Lodge. The purpose of the film is to enlighten
and inform the public as to the Ceremony's content, significance, and public·
relations value, and to enhance the public image of Freemasonry in a constructive
manner. Such a film would be equally useful for instructional purposes of Grand
Lodge Officers and for educational purposes of members at large. The film
would be made available to Constituent Lodges.
Project V: To explore the possiblity and feasibility of establishing a California
Masonic Leaming Center on or about the present facilities of the Memorial
Temple in San Francisco. Plans would include a museum, library, study rooms,
and a comprehensive learning and study program in the fields of Masonic

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

history, philosophy, psychology, religion and related subjects. Preliminary work
already done in this area has been made available to the Committee by the Grand
Secretary's office.
The Committee respectfully requests a $500.00 budget for the ensuing
Masonic year, but herein makes note that certain special projects may require
additional funds if undertaken by request of the Grand Master. The budget
requested is in addition to the film budget.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1976 Communication, one Lodge had its Dispensation continued. No
other Dispensations have been granted in the current year. We now have before
us a petition from Bicentennial Daylight Lodge U.D., requesting that a Charter
be granted.
This Lodge is located in Sacramento and holds its meetings at mid-day for the
benefit of those who work nights-or for other reasons, are unable to attend
evening meetings.
They were instituted on September 24th, just before the last Communication,
so have now had a full year of operation under dispensation. At the time they
were instituted this Committee anticipated some problems due to their small
charter membership of 29. We saw the possibility of financial problems, a
difficulty in maintaining a full corps of Officers, and in having enough members
to perform the functions of a Lodge. To counteract this, we saw great enthusiasm
and considerable Masonic experience, and we felt they could solve these
problems. We are pleased to report that our faith has been justified. While these
problems still exist, they have made a modest gain in membership and are
operating in the black. They even awarded a scholarship to a deserving student
during Public Schools week.
Early in the year they assumed responsibility for the Masonic Cornerstone
Ceremony for the Elwood Keema Center at Los Rios Community College.
Practically all of their membership participated in the arrangements and with the
help of their wives prepared the luncheon that preceeded the Ceremony. All
•
present agreed that it was a job well done.
They have submitted all their books and records covering the period under
dispensation. Normally we have suggestions for changes or improvements in the

Respectfully submitted,

Common stocks representing approximately 46% of the total market value are
widely diversified as to industry and company. During the past year performance
results were negative, with the portfolio declining in value about 5 .11 % on a
fully adjusted basis. By comparison the Dow-Jones Industrial Average declined
8.62% and the S&P 500 was down 3.64%. These figures do not include income
in the performance calculation. It may be observed that quality stocks, particularly those with more visible growth characteristics, did not perform well during
the past twelve months. Rather, companies offering a relatively high payout of
cash dividends and those engaged in basic industry operations, as compared with
consumer or scientific operations, were the better performers. Inventors currently
seem preoccupied with cash dividend income and hence securities offering this
characteristic were more in demand.
Our ·investment advisor, Alliance Capital Management Corporation, during
the year, continued to recommend securities that meet our stringent investment
objectives and policy guidelines. Your Committee is guided by the California
"Prudent Man" investment rule and the regulations of our Craft. Our basic
investment strategy is to maintain a proper balance between fixed-income and
equity securities, to buy and hold quality issues only, and to maintain recommended industry weightings within the stock portion of the portfolio.
As the economic recovery has continued, it is beginning to show signs of
fatigue as may normally be expected over long periods of time. With that concern
we have received our advisor's recommendation to maintain a relatively conservative stance, with somewhat greater emphasis upon maintaining shorter-term
investments to maintain flexibility. More than 13% of our bond portfolio matures
within 4 1h years, with an additional 25% maturing in from 41h to 91h years. We
are of the opinion that this strategy will eventually enhance the financial strength
of the portfolio as we enter a period of level ecopomic activity which in tum
furnishes an oppo'rtunity to evaluate important economic programs dealing with
energy, inflation, employment and industrial capacity. Clearly, our goal is to
provide preservation of capital with safety and dependability of income.

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1977

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The fiscal year ending June 30, 1977 saw an extension of the general economic
advance begun two years earlier. With few exceptions it was a gradual
strengthening of the economy in terms of corporate profits, personal income,
number of individuals added to the labor force, continued concern for a rate of
inflation which has proven difficult to significantly reduce, although clearly
below the double-digit level experienced a few years ago. The most significant
improvement appeared in housing starts and the value of real estate. Auto
production, a key to the economy, remained strong for the second year. Clearly,
the consumer was the key to the health of the economy. The Federal budget
deficit, although sizable, proved to be less burdensome than had earlier been
anticipated. Business spending, primarily for plant and equipment, was hesitant.
Interest rates rose to a most attractive level until March, and then tended to
declinei primarily for long-term obligations. In recent months short-term rates
have risen, chiefly because of Federal Reserve activity which permitted free
market forces of demand and supply to reflect a higher cost on borrowing and an
attempt to modify increasing iriflationary pressure. Equity prices remained
relatively stable during the last half of calendar 1976 and then began an almost
steady deterioration until June 30. In spite of that trend, the market value of the
portfolio on June 30 was $62.096 million with an estimated annual income of
$3.89 million which is a return of 6.3% on market value. Portfolio investments
remain diversified-45% in common stocks, 12% in convertible securities and
42% made up of fixed-income obligations.
The bond portfolio maintains an average weighted quality of high Aa rating,
with an average coupon of 7.35% and an average weighted maturity of 15.3
years considered to be relatively short in terms of exposure to risk for a fund with
ongoing operating characteristics.
Convertible securities offer attractive current income and the potential for
further market appreciation, generally subject to economic conditions. Current
yield on market for this sector of the account is 6.4%.

REPORT OF TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Taxation Committee exists to disseminate information concerning tax
laws. It also exists to provide advice on taxation matters when requested.
Responsibility for such matters rests with elected and appointed officers and

154

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

trustees of the various Masonic groups. The Committee has no authorization to
determine or enforce compliance with the various tax laws.
During the current year a number of tax problems have been referred to and
handled by your Committee. Your Committee stands ready to offer counsel and
advice as problems with taxing authorities develop in the future.
There are two developments this year by the Internal Revenue Service. In
March the Internal Revenue Service announced that exempt organizations, other
than private foundations, with gross receipts not normally in excess of $10,000
will not have to file Form 990 for tax years ending on or after December 31,
1976. In the past, a similar filing exemption applied to these organizations whose
gross receipts were not normally in excess of $5,000. The effect of this change
will be to relieve many Lodges and other Masonic organizations from the filing
requirement. It is, however, important to understand that this exemption does not
apply to reports due the State of California. Every Lodge and other tax exempt
organization must submit either a Form 199 or 199B to the California Franchise
Tax Board. There are no exceptions.
The other development is that the processing of tax returns has been decentralized. Previously all exempt organization material was processed by the
Philadelphia Service Center. It has now been decided that the returns for all
exempt organizations for California and Hawaii must be filed with the Fresno
Internal Revenue Service Center. All correspondence on exempt organization tax
returns must also be sent to Fresno. The result of this decentralization should be a
closer and more effective supervision over tax exempt organizations in the area.
Our Lodges, Temple Associations, and other entities may be hearing more from
the Internal Revenue Service in the future.
Each year your Taxation Committee, through you, cautions the tax exempt
organizations comprising Grand Lodge as to the importance of complying with
the various tax laws of the Federal Government and the States. In particular, the
required reports must be filed timely and accurately. Failure to file will subject
such organizations to penalties and possible loss of exempt status.
From time to time your Committee hears statements that an organization is tax
exempt because it is a nonprofit organization. Being nonprofit does not in itself
provide tax exemption status. In order to obtain tax exempt status an application
on proper forms must be submitted to the District Director of the Internal
Revenue Service and, in California, to the Franchise Tax Board. Upon approval
of the application, a Determination Letter will be sent to the applicant which
indicates the tax exempt status. It should be apparent this Determination Letter is
a most important document and should be preserved carefully in a safe and
readily accessible place. In addition to indicating the exempt status, the Internal
Revenue Service or the Franchise Tax Board may indicate special qualifications
and other vital information to the organization. From time to time your Committee finds situations where the Determination Letter is not readily available and
may be unread and the qualifications unobserved. Your Committee recommends
that officers and trustees of Grand Lodge entities and Temple Associations make
a practice of regularly referring to their Determination Letters.
It seems that each year your Committee concludes its report by again
reminding all readers of this report that tax exemption under the law is a

privil~ge. To ~aintain that privilege, we must comply with the law. Your
Taxat10n Committee stands ready to advise and assist you in this regard.

Respectfully submitted,
W. STANLEY DA VIS, Chairman

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
I
Frequently, members of this Committee have been asked by officers of Lodges
as to whether a person holding a dues receipt or other Masonic identification
from a Lodge in a foreign Jurisdiction, which we may or may not recognize, can
be admitted to or even become affiliated with a California Lodge. Such requests
for information should properly be directed to the office of the Grand Secretary
where the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges with which we are in amity
are kept. It often happens that the foreign Lodge in question is a Constituent

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Lodge of the Grand Lodge which we recognize. England, Scotland and Ireland
have subordinate Lodges all over the world as indeed do some American Grand
Lodges, such as New York. These Lodge lists are not among the records of this
Committee.

2. We have received no reply from the Grand Lodge of Acre in Brazil in
response to our request for information pertaining to their regularity, so we
suggest that we continue our surveillance of this situation.
3. The Grand Secretary for External Relations for the Grand Orient of Brazil
writes that he has noted our position on their Application for Recognition ( 1976
Proceedings, page 148) and deeply regrets our action. He further adds that all
their doors are always open to any Brother of the Grand Lodge of California
visiting Rio de Janiero or any Lodge of their Jurisdiction. This gracious gesture is
appreciated, and it is expected that a member of the Committeee will be able to
accept this invitation and better learn at first hand the other side of the dispute
between the Grand Orient and the State Grand Lodges of Brazil.
Except as noted, we are pleased to report harmony in the Masonic world.
Most Worshipful, I move the adoption of this report and its suggestions and
recommendations.

Matters of serious import threaten the Grand Orient of Italy, Palazzo Giustiniani, which we recognize. The "Family of Piazza del Gesu," which had

GRAND ORATION

Masonry is a sacred band of friends and Brothers wherein we are taught many
great truths and important moral and spiritual lessons in order that we may divest
our hearts and consciences of all the vices and superfluities of life, and thereby fit
our minds as living stones for that spiritual building, that house not made with
hands, eternal in the Heavens. Masonry's cause for existence is to provide
challenge, encouragement, and strength toward enabling a man to achieve his
highest and best according to the designs laid down upon the trestleboard for his
life by the Supreme Grand Master of the Universe . Inseparably related to a man's
personal development is his concern for the welfare of his family, his Brethren,
his community, his Nation, and his concern for society the world around.
Recall with me the conclusion of the Third Degree when the Master of the
Lodge extends congratulations to the newly-raised Master Mason by saying:
"The eyes of the Fraternity are now upon you; be just, be faithful, be true,
and convince the world by your acts that on becoming a Master Mason you
have become a better man."
This is the essence of Masonry ... to challenge men to changed lives, to
inspire them to achieve their noblest and highest, and to motivate them to indeed
become better men. I will grant you that there is much more to Masonry, but it is
my frrm conviction that if we fail to pre-eminently teach the great moral and
spiritual truths within Masonry, and if we fail to inspire men and bring them
closer to the Almighty God of the Universe, then our temples become hollow,
echoing caverns, and our ritual becomes as resounding brass and tinkling
cymbals! With this as our concept of Masonry, let us take a look at our Fraternity
today.
There are those among us who see Masonry today as on a downhill slide,
decreasing in number of members while the average age of members is
increasing-a Fraternity that has passed its' zenith and is now waning. Closely
akin are others among us who seem content to reminisce over past achievements
of Masonry, proudly basking in the reflected glory of great Masonic history.
They see their role in Masonry today as guardians of the past, "protecting" the
Fraternity fron1 change, obsessed with the preservation of the forms, the ritual,
and regulations. To all of these Brethren let me emphatically say that selfpresevation- mere survival-is not of itself sufficient justification for Masonry
to continue.
Let me assure you that I do not lack reverence for the past. It is with gratitude
and respect that I recall the heritage in which we stand, and it is indeed time that
we rededicate ourselves to the great principles of Masonry that have withstood
the ravages of barbarous attack. Let us, with grateful appreciation, honor those
Brethren who have walked this pathway with distinction-g reat leaders of our
Fraternity, a number of whom are here present today, whose zeal and dedicated
service make it possible for us to gather here in.this Annual Communication.
During this past bi-centennial year we have been reminded on numerous
occasions of the vital part our Masonic forefathers have had in the formation and
development of om: beloved Country, founded on the principles we hold dear of
equality, liberty, and justice for all. We should look well to the past. but not as
shackles or restraints upon the present. Rather, the past is the ground floor, the
second, and third stories of the edifice upon which we now continue to build the

my fmal opportunity to address you as your Grand Orator, 1t 1s my fervent hope

. ·
Volumes have been written on the meaning of Masonry, its message, its
teachings, and the interpretation of its' allegory. While I recognize the im~ss~­
bility of adequately defining Masonry in a few sentences, never-the-less 1t is
important to your understanding of what I wish to say today that I first attempt to
state what I believe to be the very heart of Masonry.

temple of Masonry to ever increasing heights. May we never be burdened down
by the grandeur of the past; instead, may the past give us a perspective from
which we can more clearly view the present and provide challenge and inspiration for the future.
As we recall the greatness of Masonry in past history, let us consider why we
pay particular tribute to certain Masons of distinction. We honor those of our
Brethren whose lives and deeds in the world exemplify the teachings of the Craft
which they learn in the lodgeroom. Neither the man of lofty thoughts who
remains in a closet nor the man of feverish activity who lacks clarity of purpose
and inner direction are worthy of our acclaim. Recall in the Holy Writings, in the
E~istle of James, we read: ''.Thou hast faith, and I have works; shew me thy faith
without thy works, and I will shew thee my, faith by my works." As with faith
so it is with the principles of Masonry. It is the man whose faith and high ideal~
are evidenced in his actions who is deserving of our recognition. We honor
George Washington because he was a man of high principles and lofty vision
who also had the courage and strength to translate those inner convictions into a
life of noble action. His life of leadership and his accomplishments for our
N~tion stand as irrefutable testimony to his beliefs. Let me suggest that a
umversal characteristic of all Masons of distinction is an unfaltering fidelity to
their innermost convictions and the courage to live in accord with those
convictions, in ·word and in deed, without regard for public opinion, political
pressures, or personal consequences.
What is the greatest threat to Masonry today? It is not members growing older
nor declining Lodge memberships. The greatest threat to Masonry today is a lack
of the courage to conduct our affairs within the lodgeroom and before the world
in a manner consistent with the tenets and virtues we espouse to believe. Hence, I
confront you with the question, "Courage ... or Conformity?" Which will be
the characteristic ascribed to us, to the Grand Lodge of California in 1977 and
1978, by future historians? Will we be remembered as men of courage or of
complacent conformity?
Let me explain just what I mean by courage. I am speaking not so much of the
courage needed to face physical danger from external threats, but rather of
courage as the inner side of growth and maturity-the capacity to meet and
conquer the anxiety which arises when facing the unknown. Think of courage as
that inner strength which enables a man to speak and act with firm conviction in
accord with his beliefs, yet with humility and without rebellion. On the other
hand, lack of courage is to compromise one's deepest convictions in order to
conform to the situation of the moment, to give the appearance of concurrence
with the ppinions of another person or group. Let me hasten to assure you that I
am in no way advocating a negativistic non-conformity or non-conformity for its
own sake. A harmonious unity of thought is a desirable characteristic for all
societies, especially for Masonry. I am simply saying that conformity at the
expense of personal integrity is lack of courage.
Courage is required all along the pathway of growth and development. For the
youth, courage is required to break from the ties of the infantile past. For the man
of more seasoned years, it takes courage to break from the old and familiar in
order that the new can be born. The crest of courage in this age of conformity is

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

163

the integrity to stand true to one's own convictions, not defiantly or in the posture
of rebellion, but simply and steadfastly because this is what one believes.
Courage is the affirmative choice, not acquiesence because there are no alternatives. With this concept of courage in mind, why do I say that lack of courage is
the greatest threat to Masonry today?
I dare say that there is not a man among us in this Annual Communication who
would not have the courage to stand firmly for freedom of speech, freedom of
assembly, freedom of worship .. . these which we might label "external
freedoms." But do we have the courage to preserve our "inner freedom" ...
the courage to be true and faithful in our actions to the innermost, God-given
beliefs and convictions within our hearts? Do we have the ability, and do we
devote the necessary time and effort, to think through and evaluate a given
situation in relationship to the fundamental purposes and objectives of Masonry
which we summarized a few moments ago? Do we stop to consider a proposed
course of action in the light of the three principal tenets of brotherly love, relief,
and truth and the four cardinal virtues of temperance, fortitude, prudence, and
justice? Then, having sorted out the essential from the trivial and reached a
conclusion as to what we really believe to be the truth of the issue at hand, do we
then have the courage to take action to implement our beliefs, or do we then,
having arrived at an understanding of what we believe to be the truth, allow
expediency or complacency to over-rule integrity when it comes to the words we
speak or the actions we take?
In a society governed by Watergate morals and an ethic of expediency,
Masonry must stand true to its principal tenets, proclaim duty to the Supreme
Architect of the Universe as man's first allegiance, and affirm compassion and
brotherly love as the guiding quality in the relationship of man to man. We need
the courage to proclaim the eternal truths of Masonry to the world in clear and
unmistakable termsr and of equal importance, we must proclaim these truths in
language that is understood by the world today. Masonry is too often content to
mumble to itself rather than to speak relevantly to the world. By that I mean to
say that we tend to focus our attention and effort on what goes on within the
lodgeroom-on the repetition of ritual and the conferral of degrees-rather than
challenging and motivating the Brethren to live as Masons before the world so
that family, neighbors, and business associates will indeed observe that upon
becoming a Master Mason we have become better men. The world is groping for
men of high moral standards, men of integrity, men who are concerned and
involved with the desparate needs of present society. But all too often we present
to them a Masonry that conveys the image of beautiful ritual, impressive
ceremonies, and officers with high-sounding titles . . . an image of selfaggrandizement rather than of ministry to the needs or our fellowmen. The world
recognizes men who are able to translate their lofty ideals into noble lives and
actions relevant to contemporary society. But we so often speak to the world in
terms of the patterns of past decades which may no longer have their previous
dynamic impact or even be relevant today. Thus we may be mumbling to
ourselves and failing to communicate to the world at all, or at best, sending out a
message that is confusing and bewildering. Her me carefully, for I am in no way
saying that we should lower our standards and ideals to conform to the society in

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to submit its annual report for
the 1976-1977 Grand Lodge Year. It is the Committee's opinion that seldom
have the Brethren who are charged with the responsibility of providing Temples
for our Lodges faced greater challenges. The constantly increasing cost of
construction, maintenance, utilities, taxes, more stringent building and safety
codes, together with the ravages of time on the older Temples, has made it
increasingly more difficult to operate Temples within their income. The serious
impact of the problems is exemplified by the Committee having received only
one application for the construction of a new Temple this year.
The Committee and the Grand Master have placed great emphasis on seeking
solutions to those cases where Temples are experiencing financial difficulty, or
where extensive and urgently necessary repairs are beyond their financial
capability. Your Committee is encouraged by the thoroughness with which the
Lodges have approached these problems, and the initiative they have shown in
seeking solutions to their problems.
Your Committee emphasizes the autonomy of each Lodge or Temple Association in respect to Temple operations. It is vitally important that the Brethren of
the Lodges recognize that it is ultimately their responsibility to provide and
maintain the Temples, and that rental increases to all tenants of the building are
often the only solution to provide funds for Temple operations. It is highly
probable that rental increases will result in dues increases for the Lodges and
other bodies using the Temple. This, too, should be recognized as a reality.
Your Committee firmly believes that the problem of financing Temple
operations will continue to grow. In order to provide greater assistance to the

Respectfully submitted,
KEITH V. JOHNSON, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
During this past year, your Committee on Public Schools has continued many
of the programs that have been effective and has implemented several new
concepts. The hard working Committee consisted of thirty members.
We had the enthusiastic support and encouragement of our Grand Master,
Most Worshipful Kermit A. Jacobson and the Grand Lodge Elective Officers,
with whom your Chairman met on numerous occasions throughout the year. To
them and the Grand Secretary's office, particularly Marion Thomas in the Supply
Room, we express our thanks for the abundant cooperation extended to our
Committee. Our liaison Officer has been Right Worshipful Vernon Gordon who
has a deep and profound interest in our Public Schools. His counsel and guidance
this past year have been greatly appreciated.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The concept of having six Division Coordinators and several Committeemen
working with each of the Division Coordinators worked well and covered,
geographicaly, California and Hawaii to assure that every Lodge be personally
contacted by a Committeeman offering assistance. In order to better accomplish
the duties of this Committee, it is suggested that the maximum number of
Committee members be increased to forty by resolution at the 1978 Grand Lodge
Communication.
The Grand Master proclaimed April as Public Schools Month and encouraged
Masonic Lodges to be in contact with their local school Departments to designate
a week during April as PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK in their locality for the 1977
Observance based on the theme PUBLIC SCHOOLS -LEARNI NG FOR LIVING. This outstanding slogan for 1977 met with great acceptance throughout our
Jurisdiction. Many cornerstones and plaques reflect the profound message that
our Public Schools are truly the place for LEARNIN G FOR LIVING. The
cooperation of public officials and school administrators resulted in numerous
supporting proclamations and pronouncements of Public Schools Week, reaching
far and wide to the general public.
Two full Committee meetings and one Division Coordinators' meeting were
held during this past Grand Lodge year. The Public Schools Support guidelines
in the Lodge Manual were updated and distributed to all Lodges. This document,
when used by the local Public Schools Committee, can be of immeasureable help
in promoting and planning local public schools week observances.
