On April 11, 1977 the Los Angeles Unified School District wrote to our Grand
Lodge soliciting our assistance in recruiting workers for their DOVES (dedicated
older volunteers for educational services) program. To this end our Grand Master
sent a letter to the 27 ,000 Masons living in the Los Angeles Unified School
District urging them, their families and friends to explore the District's DOVES
project and to help with the recruitment of retirees as volunteers. Cards were
enclosed with the Grand Master's July 22, 1977 letter to be completed and
returned. The response with the cards and phone calls was most gratifying, and
on Wednesday October 5, 1977 several hundred DOVES and volunteers assembled in Los Angeles and were greeted by our Grand Master and started their
orientation to become DOVES. This is an outstanding pilot project and establishes a year-round Public Schools Program for our Grand Lodge. Letters were
also sent to the Masters of the 139 Lodges within the area of the School District
urging their support. Follow up letters will be sent to the Masters soon.
Your Committee has now received requests from the Santa Monica School
District and Long Beach School District for the same type of involvement from
our Grand Lodge. The Board of Trustees of the San Francisco School Department has also requested that we assist them in forming citizen advisory groups
and assist in their volunteer programs.

GENERAL COMMENTS

Concern was expressed this past year that we as Masons and also as
individuals do not and cannot condone some of the things that are presently being
done in our local schools, and that we must be careful not to let the general public
be of the opinion that we support all the actions and programs of our school
districts. What we do support is the concept of PUBLIC EDUCATION and not
the specific programs of a particular school district. The 1978 posters will say
SUPPORT PUBLIC EDUCATION to help bring this important point into focus.
Concern is felt by the Public Schools Committee that some Lodges, particularly in the metropolitan areas, consider that they have accomplished their
Masonic duty and responsibility by participating in a large joint effort with other
Lodges and/or Districts in a Public Schools Observance. The Committee congratulates these Lodges on their joint participation and encourages their continuance, but wishes to remind each Lodge that there are numerous April and
year round projects for individual Lodge participation. The Committee encourages each Lodge to have a "project of their own." Many ideas and suggestions
are contained in the green Public Schools Support Guidelines in the Lodge
Manual.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
INFORMATION AND RESPONSIBILITY
MASONIC

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
During the year 1976-77 the Committee has been restored to full strength of 30
members by the M. W. Grand Master, Kermit A. Jacobson. The result has
enabled us to carry the Committee programs generally throughout the states of
this Jurisdiction.
Several of the Committee's earlier programs have continued to be used by
Lodges even though not currently being promoted. These are programs which
have been found useful by the Lodge officers.
Two programs have been used during this term: 1) Candidates' Education, and
2) Leadership. Most of the Committee has been involved in the former,
explaining the purpose of the program to Lodge officers, Inspectors and
Coaches. Reception of the program has been spotty. Neither all Masters nor all
Inspectors are convinced that Candidates require education as to the purposes of
Freemasonry, the policies of the Grand Lodge, or explanation of what the Ritual
is supposed to teach.
Those Lodges which have adopted such a series of information sessions, have
found an increase in attendance, and in participation of their new members. They
have also, not surprisingly, found increased interest in Lodge outside activities.
We expect to discover an increase in numbers of applications also, but cannot yet
document this.
As was expected, resistance to the program is generally found in Lodges with
few activities and few candidates. Fortunately we have found that in areas where
there has been cooperation among the Masters, the Inspectors and Committeemen, the program has been better than 50% successful. This should be
considered good for a voluntary program in its first year. This program should be
continuous if its benefits are to be realized in the California Jurisdiction.
As partially reported in the California Freemason, the Leadership Program this
year has been conducted in conjunction with the Ritual Committee. As of the
time this report is being written, there have been 12 such meetings held. They
were located in Redding, Ukiah, North Sacramento, Oakland, San Francisco,
Modesto, Fresno, Santa Maria, Oxnard, Bellflower, Long Beach and Los
Angeles.
The program is aimed at the officers of the Constituent Lodges, and planned to
inspire them to take the ideas presented and to fit them to the conditions in their

177

own Lodges. In many cases, officers have stayed until after the close of the
session to ask if an idea of theirs would be acceptable. And that is what we have
actually sought to happen. The officers have been struck with an idea of their
own to promote the welfare of their own Lodges. In only one case did an officer
completely miss the point: he thought the case histories used to describe methods
of leadership were frivolous! While we lost audience following the morning
Ritual Committee meeting and lunch, we seldom lost a man who started the
afternoon session.
~e public r~lations work undertaken both within Lodges and to the general
pubh~ has .contmued. These talks are made to Churchs, Service Clubs, Lodges,
Scottish Rite, York Rite, Chambers of Commerce, High Twelve Clubs, Eastern
Star an~ T?astmistresses. None of them are a hard sell for Masonry; most of them
are patriotic; all of them mention Masonry.
We have been ably assisted in our work by several dedicted Masons who are
not members of the Committee: W. and M. W. Brothers, Adams, Bates,
Berliner, Chapman, Ebbage, Herbold, Long, MacPhee, Meriam, Nocas, Settlemyer and Thurmond.
We are also indebted to the M. W. Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., and Grand
Secretary, W. Verne Hendrix, Assistant Grand Secretary, and many of the Grand
Lodge office staff for their assistance in not only their regular duties, but also for
extracurricular work in handling foreign Grand Lodge correspondence and
arrangements and requests, and the many demands we have had to make on their
time.

Constituent Lodges and the Brethren.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History was engaged in the following activities
during the past year:
1. A letter was sent to the Masters of the Lodges suggesting that they write
their respective Lodges' histories for the Bicentennial Year of 1976. The
yearly history of one of the Lodges in this jurisdiction, as well as a
checklist, were enclosed with the letter to assist the Lodges in this
endeavor. The Committee members encouraged the Lodges in their areas
and assisted those which requested aid.
2. At the request of the Grand Master, the Committee surveyed a representative number of Lodges to determine the feasibility of the Grand Lodge
re-printing the book, "Gold Dust and Trowels". This charming book
relates the history and background of most of the first 100 Lodges in both
text and pictures. The Committee recommended that the book be reprinted by the Grand Lodge.
3. The Tuolumne County Clerk and Historian requested that the Grand Lodge
assist him in determining if an early Mother Lode building was in fact one
of the first Masonic Temples in this State. The Committee investigated the
request, provided information and made certain investigatiye suggestions
to the Tuolumne County Clerk and Historian. Should subsequent research
be fruitful and establish that the building was the Masonic Temple of
Mount Jefferson Lodge No. 107 (now extinct), a plaque may be placed
upon the building with the agreement of all concerned.
4. The Committee researched Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, the senior Mother
Lode Lodge, and the three extinct Lodges (Columbia No. 28, George
Washington No. 62 and Mount Jefferson No. 107) that consolidated with
it for the purpose of creating an interesting display at the Grand Lodge
Communication in October 1977. It will be titled ''The Anatomy of a
Mother Lode Lodge."
5. The Committee investigated the worthiness of the request of Benicia
Lodge No. 5 to have the Grand Lodge forgive $5,000.00 of its loan from
the Grand Lodge for the restoration of its original Temple of 1850 vintage.
The Committee recommended that the $5,000.00 be forgiven in light of
the following circumstances: (a) This first Temple is located in a very
historic community and presents Masonry in a very favorable light, (b) it is
and will be used by many Lodges for visitations, (c) it has been and is a
financial burden to Benicia Lodge considering that Benicia Lodge also
maintains its current Temple, (d) Benicia Lodge will be doing further
internal restoration work and obtaining period furnishings and (e) Benicia
Lodge members have a very positive and determined attitude to see this
project through to its conclusion.
6. The Committee provided the Grand Master with California Masonic
History information at his request.
7. The Committee provided the Lodges and the Brethren with California
Masonic History information upon their request.

The Committee is particularly grateful to the California FREEMASON for
publishing in its quarterly publication many of the unusual developments in other
Jurisdictions.
Membership was on the upswing in the deep South, while the rest of the nation
showed a loss of members. Of the 58 Grand Jurisdictions (in the USA and
Canada), 47 revealed a decrease. Eight had an increase. There were 15,332
Lodges, with a total membership of 3,510,225 -a decrease of 41,543 since
1975. States registering the greatest gains were: So. Carolina-1 ,872;
Tennessee -881; Florida-82 1; No. Carolina- 520 and Arizona-1 56.
New York with 6,910 led with the largest Masonic membership decreases,
followed by lllinois-4, 910; California -3,423; Michigan- 3,081 and
Ohio-2,57 2.
The greatest Masonic membership is found in Ohio with 250, 136 members,
followed by Pennsylva nia-229,93 6; Texas-226 ,619; California -213, 137 and
New York-201 ,695.
The condition of the Craft appears to be healthy in most sections of the United
States. In Canada, a number of rural Lodges are suffering from lack of new
members, China, Mexico and Nova Scotia are giving a great deal of ground work
in simplified teaching methods of the Ritual.
Many Jurisdictions attribute their increases in membership to realistic, wellorganized and supervised leadership and Educational programs.
A number of Grand Lodges have viable programs to educate their new
candidates and members. Elective Line Officers in Lodges attend weekly classes
for further training to become skillful and professional leaders.
Tennessee has a full-time Director of Education to direct its Leadership and
Educational programs. North Carolina has an Education Officer for each of its
districts.
In many communities, Masonry was the subject of praise-worthy publicity. As
part of its Sunday edition, the Toledo, Ohio "BLADE" published a 16-pp.
rotogravure section devoted entirely to Masonry and was distributed with
218,000 copies of the newspaper.
The Grand Lodge of Scotland has avilable in Braille five Ritual .books
published for Freemasons by the Royal National Institute for the Blind.
One idea stands out with deep clarity. There are two major problems which
seem to plague Masonry in practically every part of the United States and in
many foreign areas-apat hy and communication. The first can only be rectified
by a renewal of spirit and commitment by the Masters, the Wardens and Past
Masters.
The usual basic remedies are suggested; Lodges should plan events, sponsor
interesting programs, appoint Committees that will function. Lodges need new
members in order to survive. There is no easy way to assure this point; put the
Brethren to work is the most sensible idea propounded.
Lines of communication are composed of Lodge Trestleboards, program of
events posted in the Tyler's room, "word-of-m outh" enthusiasm, and utilizing
as many Brethren- old and new alike-to serve on Lodge functions.
In a number of states, it was noted that more Masonic Lodges are taking an
active part in community efforts. Freemasonry's usefulness is the cumulative and

collective efforts of its members. Masonry must not compete with service clubs.
Mason.s can do a lot to uphold their basic ideas by working on civic, patriotic,
educational and athletic groups in their areas.
Innumerable Lodges have programs which encourage the participation in
youth. programs ...A half dozen states have set up the age of 18 as deemed
sufficient to pet1t1on for membership. Reduced membership fees, as tried by
several states, have not been instrumental of gaining large increases in personnel.
In a number of states, "suspensio ns" still outnumber the "demits."
Educatio~al programs- workshops for training of Lodge Officers and
leaders-w ill ~nng about a renewed and revitalized interest in Freemasonry.
The Committee has had an interesting assignment in ferreting out news of
importance to California Grand Lodge leaders. The publication in the FREEMASON of our findings serves as an inspiration to work with greater effort.

REPORT OF
COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM

REGULATIONS GOVERNING ORGANIZATIONS

OF THE
MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND LODGE F. & A.M. OF CALIFORNIA

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Commercialism submits herewith its report for the Masonic
Year 1977.
The chronic problems of the unauthorized use of Square & Compass and
commercial ventures has subsided dramatically in the past year. The Committee
has been confronted with less than a handful of such occurrences. The decrease
can be attributed to the wider-spread publicity the problem has received in the
past few years-or a failure on the part of the Members to recognize a situation
and report it. There has been a greater number of inquiries by Inspectors during
the planning stages of apparent commercial ventures which has alleviated the
problems involving commercial ventures.
Three years ago this Committee undertook the task of rewriting the Commercialism Regulations. Many of the Committeemen who were the original authors
of various parts of the Report are no longer members of the Committee. We
particularly want to express appreciation to George Nelson who was the original
author of what has become Part I of the Regulations. Special recognition is called
to Robert Simon, the original author of what has become Part II of the
Regulations.
Several Past Grand Masters have also contributed.
A special thank you goes to Leo Anderson who painstakingly reviewed,
reread, and, in the final analysis, rewrote large portions to conform to Masonic
law and policy.
Attached to this Report are the proposed Regulations which this Committee
submits to Grand Lodge as the ''Regulations Governing Organizations subject to
the Jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California."
This Committee expresses its appreciation for the helpful cooperation of the
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and all Grand Lodge Officers.

Respectfully submitted,

The following regulations are adopted to preclude violations of the California
Masonic Code by organizations subject to the jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, by reason of requiring Masonic
membership, affiliation or sponsorship.
PART I
COMMERCIALISM REGULATIONS RELATING TO
ADULT ORDERS

1. The term "organization" as used in Part I is defined to include:

a) any Constituent Lodge;
b) any group, chapter, order, club, association or organization, requiring
Masonic affiliation or sponsorship, including but not limited to:
Eastern Star
York Rite Bodies
Order of Amaranth
Scottish Rite Bodies
White Shrine of Jerusalem
Shrine
Social Order of Beauceant
Shrine Clubs
Masonic Oubs
Sciots
Grotto
2. These regulations apply to all Master Masons residing within the jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, irrespective
of whether such •Master Mason is a member of a Lodge in California or
elsewhere.
REGULATIONS

I.
ADVERTISING

No Lodge, or member of a Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print
advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to be
Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body, order, or
organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership. Anything to the contrary notwithstanding, there may be printed in charity football
game programs only sponsored by organizations requiring Masonic membership
as a prerequisite for membership therein, when the proceeds of the game go to a
Masonic or Masonic related charity, complimentary advertisements, such as
" with name
" or "Best Wishes from
"Compliments of
of individuals or companies inserted in the blanks, but not naming any product as
such, and provided that the proceeds from such advertisements shall not exceed
the cost of printing and mailing or distributing such programs and that such
advertising shall be subject to rules and regulations of the Committee on
Commercialism of this Grand Lodge.

187

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is proper for a Lodge to print in a program the name of sponsors who
contributed to the success of an event. A Lodge may announce in a Lodge
bulletin the name of a speaker or entertainer, that person's business affiliation
and background in order to stimulate interest in a Lodge program.
This regulation does not prohibit the placement in bona fide newspapers of
legitimate news items of organization, group or club activities or advertisements
in said newspapers in connection with rummage sales which do not use the name
of any of the organizations hereinbefore named or any group thereof.

tion from voluntarily donating such a gift or contributing to a charity, or
furnishing entertainment for a meeting of the organization, either individually or
through his business. If the organization wishes to announce the name and
business of the member who sponsored or furnished the entertainment at the
meeting, it may do so.

186

IV.
COMMERCIAL VENTURES

II.
PUBLIC SUPPORT

No organization as herein defined nor any agency thereof such as social clubs,
mothers' clubs, sewing circles or other clubs or groups within such organization,
nor any member thereof, using any name whatever, shall sponsor any event,
project, scheme or plan wherein public support is requested or solicited on behalf
of such organization or any group thereof and tickets or other items may not be
sold to the general public except as otherwise provided herein. Rummage sales
wherein public support is solicited in the name of the organization or of any
group thereof are forbidden, and these sales may not be held in a Masonic
Temple. However, organizations may hold rummage sales which are open to the
public but the place of sale may not display the name of the organization
conducting the sales. News stories or advertisements of the sales may be used but
may not contain the name of the organization holding the sales.
Merchants or other members of the public may not be solicited for merchandise or other donations to the sale.
This regulation does not prohibit the sales of tickets to members, their families
or friends, for breakfasts, dinners, card parties, dances, bazaars, and so forth.
These breakfasts, etc., may be held in Masonic Temples or elsewhere, but should
always be handled well within the bounds of propriety and no invitation to attend
may be extended to the public as such. There may be a news story in the local
press to the effect that the organization is having a dinner or whatever the event
may be, but this story may not refer to any charge for the affair and may not
indicate that the public is invited to attend. Merchants or other members of the
public may not be solicited to buy tickets, participate or make donations of any
kind .
Public support may be asked of activities if the entire proceeds less necessary
expenses for food, etc., are actually given to a recognized charity of the
Fraternity or of the organization.
III.
SOLICITATION OF GIFTS

The solicitation of merchants, firms, business houses, or the public for gifts of
merchandise, money or prizes of any kind for or in connection with the general
activities of the group or organization, such as dinners, parties, and meetings, is
strictly forbidden . This regulation does not prohibit a member of any organiza-

No organization herein defined or any agency or group thereof shall directly or
indirectly engage in any business, project, venture, promotion, scheme or plan
which is unethical, misleading, fraudulent or illegal. No such organization shall
knowingly receive money or property as a donation or contribution from such
operations. (C.M.C. 2066).

v.
GAMBLING

No organization as herein defined nor any member or group of members
thereof shall directly or indirectly give aid or countenance to any raffle, lottery,
or other gambling enterprise or accept any of the proceeds or profits therefrom.
(C.M.C. 3314).
Door prizes are permissible only if those attending do not pay anything of
value for the chance to receive the door prize. In this connection the payment of
the usual charge of the restaurant or organization serving a dinner, lunch, or
breakfast is not the payment of something of value for the privilege of drawing
and the door prizes must be of nominal value and may be donated by members of
the organization.
Table or score prizes at card parties may be given if the prizes are donated by
the members of the organization and are of nominal value.
In case of doubt or disagreement as to the applicability of these regulations to
any particular event or enterprise, consultation should be had with the Inspector
of the District. There are a number of decisions on subjects covered in these
Regulations in the 1958 Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, commencing on page

25.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A .M. of California:

In now our 190th year since the Consitution was signed, on Sept. 17, 1787 by
39 delegates of the Constitutional Convention, we are still living under the Rights
and Freedom guaranteed by this document.
The Constitution was not a radical document but was the result of practical
experience as well as knowledge of political theory and history . The basic
principle of the Constitution is that supreme power resides in the people and is
delegated by the people to the government. The government must respect the
rights of the people and render an accowit to them.

190

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

With many of the signees of the Constitution being men well known for their
leadership, for their part in creating a new nation; they were also well known for
their Masonic activities. Thus, with this Masonic background, is there any
wonder that we Masons in California and Hawaii still promote the month of
September as the month to again make all people of the States aware of this
amazing document that has stood the test of time.
President McKinley stated that the Constitution is a sacred instrument, and a
sacred trust is given to us to see that its preservation in all its virtue and vigor is
passed on to the generations yet to come. This still stands today. The history of
its accomplishments and of our people have been an inspiration that has
stimulated love of country, loyalty and patriotism in the minds and hearts of the
generations of Americans who have preceded us. Now it is up to us as Masons to
plant in the minds of our young people these same virtues, love of _country,
loyalty and patriotism so that they may pass it on to the next generation after
them.
The Grand Master reconstructed the Committee this year along the same idea
as the Grand Lodge Committee on Homes Endowment. The membership was
increased from 13 to 37, including a Consultant and a Chairman. This was to
give the State better coverage where each Committeeman would not have so
many Lodges in his district to contact, and for better communication. It worked
very well. Many fine programs were initiated throughout the State. Hawaii had a
splendid program planned. At this time, all the results are not in, but those
received have shown marked improvement over past years. Many Committeemen have devoted long hours of work, and are to be complimented on their
devotion to Masonry. Unfortunately, many Lodges did not participate, and these
should receive even greater attention next year. It has been a year that I
personally have enjoyed and hope the Committeemen have had the same
pleasure. Next year will be one of greater dedication, participation and much
improvement. There is an inspiring message in this year's Proclamation issued
by our Grand Master, Kermit A. Jacobson, and I feel that all of us should not
only read it, but read it again and accept the challenge it contains.
I wish to thank all of my Committeemen and Lodges that took part in this
year's Constitution Observance programs. In conclusion, I would ask all present
to remember William Tyler Page's "The American Creed" - "I believe in the
United States of America as a government of the people, by the people and for
the people, whose just powers are derived at the consent of the governed; a
democracy in a republic, a sovereign nation of many sovereign states; a perfect
union, one and inseparable, established upon those principles of freedom,
equality, justice and humanity for which American patriots sacrificed their lives
and fortunes."
I therefore believe it is my duty to my country to love it, to support its
Constitution, to obey its laws, to respect its flag, and to defend it against all
enemies.
The Committee stands ready to do everything possible to encourage even more
programs in 1978.

.
To the Most Worshipfal Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is doing and giving for somebody else,
on this all life's splendors depend,
and joys of this world when you sum them all up,
are found in the love of your family and friends:
Truly our Masonic Youth Orders are part of our great Masonic family, and it
behooves each one of us to become friends with these dedicated and inspiring
young people.
The accomplishments and objectives adopted for the Committee on Youth
Activities, (reference the 1976 Proceedings) have all been accomplished during
this past year. A copy of the statement of purpose and objectives is attached to
this report.
Quarterly meetings of this Committee were held in both the Northern and
Southern parts of this Jurisdiction with intermittent special meetings, as required
to accomplish specific assignments and activities. The attendance by Committee
members at these meetings was most gratifying.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee undertook a geographical study of the Jurisdiction in an
attempt to coordinate Committee members Inspectoral Districts, and the youth
organizations on a local level. The result of this study is a geographical and
Inspectoral District assignment for each member of this Committee. Hopefully
the end result will be that each Committeeman has the opportunity to better serve
this Grand Lodge and members of the youth organizations. A copy of the
1976-77 assignments is attached along with a map of the State indicating the
location of each Committee member, and his assigned Districts and area.
Rent has always been a subject of discussion whenever more than one youth
organization or youth leader gets together. Many Past Grand Masters have
addressed themselves to the particular problem of high ~ents with regards to
individual youth organizations. Knowing the problems facing our Temple Boards
and Temple Corporations in these times of inflation and increasing c.ost~, yo~r
Committee on Youth Activities endeavored to assist the youth organizations m
understanding the problems facing the Temple Corporations, and also to assist
the Temple Corporations and the Temple Associations in further unders.tanding
the problems besetting our youth organizations with regards to the ever mcreasing costs in our society. Some rents were reduced, some remained as they were,
but all hopefully better understood the problems the other faced in trying to
survive.
Lodges were encouraged by Committee members to support youth ~r~ani~a­
tions in a more visible manner. Their need is more to have adult parbcipat10n
than the monetary contributions so often given in lieu of participation. This has
proved successful as an endeavor of this Committee and hopefully a better
understanding of the needs of the youth organizations has been the end result.
San Juan Lodge, No. 732, displayed their strong support for the youth
organizations when they voted to move their Lodge meeting place, rather than_ t?
desert their youth groups when time and space became a problem. Truly the spmt
of Masonic brotherhood and the Masonic family lives well in San Juan Lodge.
Some Districts have joined together with the Inspector and visited youth
meetings as a group, which is certainly an encouraging sign as both young _and
young in heart appear to enjoy this type of activity. W~ s~cerely recom~~nd it to
all the Lodges and Districts that have a youth group withm a close proxtmi~. We
believe that this will further assist the programs of the Grand Lodge, but will also
prove to be a most inspiring activity for the Lodge members .
.
City wide seminars were prepared and conducted by Committee members
using a Grand Lodge approved program and format to foster a better understanding of how the Grand Lodge, local Lodg~, and Maso~ in general operates.
This program proved to be very beneficial and many times the question ~d
answer period at the conclusion of the seminar lasted longer than the semmar
itself, and the interest of the young people in Masonry certainly supports the
supportive position of this Grand Lodge with regard to the youth orders.
.
Much time and effort on the Resolution passed at the 1976 Annual Commurucation providing guidelines for more liberal fund raising programs. for_ the youth
organizations, hopefully has resulted in an acceptable set of guidehnes to be
approved at this Communication. Certainl~ there is much con~u~ion throughout
this Jurisdiction on how the current regulabons relate to the actlvity of the youth

organizations with regards to fund raising. This Committee worked with the Ad
Hoc Committee formed by our Grand Master, and also the Committee on
Commercialism, and our sincere thanks and appreciation goes to Past Grand
Master Leo E. Anderson, Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee and Past
Grand Master Theodore Meriam, Chairman of the Policy and General Purposes
Committee, for their support, guidance, and assistance in this most difficult task.
This Committee encourages its members to be active with local youth
organi~ations, and in many cases averaged more than 12 nights per month, per
Committee member. These included youth meetings, dinners, installations, car
washes, and other fund raising and fun projects. Again, this proved a most
worthwhile activity for Committee members and further fostered an understanding between members of our Grand Lodge and the local youth organizations.
A special effort was made to encourage Masons to become active as advisors
on adult councils and boards. In most cases the youth organizations require that
board members be a member of the Masonic Fraternity, and in many cases only
one or two local Masons have been carrying the load for the statutory requirement of six or more. This program appears also to be assisting the youth
organ~zations in obtaining their one big need, namely-People. We encourage
Consbtuent Lodges to assist in providing much needed leadership.
A specific assignment was received by your Committee on Youth Activities,
this being the special youth program and banquet scheduled for Wednesday
evening of this Annual Communication. We encourage all attending this Annual
Communication to participate, as it will be a wonderful opportunity to share the
joy of our Masonic Youth Groups and enjoy these outstanding youth leaders.
With the assistance of our Grand Secretary, and under the direction of Most
Worshipful Kermit Jacobson our Grand Master, a banquet has been arranged
with special entertainment and a presentation of the elected leaders of the youth
organizations from•throughout this Grand Jurisdiction. A special salute to our
Grand Master for undertaking this original and most unique activity.
A new brochure was designed to be used in all Lodges outlining the individual
youth orders and brief history and statement of purpose. This brochure can be
inexpensively reproduced and is designed to be used by Lodges to make their
membership aware of the youth group opportunities available to them and their
families.
Membership problems are not new to the Masonic Fraternity and our youth
groups are experiencing great difficulty due to the many areas of competition.
We encourage Lodges to assist with membership programs of local organizations
by publishing articles, where proper, in trestle-boards by appointing a Youth
Committeeman within the Lodge and allowing a report to be made at Stated
Meetings to allow a better awareness of the youth organizations and their specific
problems within a local area, and also by frequent visits of Lodge members to the
local youth organizations.
History was made September 10, 1977 as the Officers ofthis Grand Lodge laid
the Cornerstone at the new DeMolay headquarters in Southern California. The
"Dream" as it has been dubbed, is a beautiful edifice, containing a Chapel,
conference room, general office area, and beautiful park which will serve as the
home for DeMolay in Southern California. The park has a replica of the Fountain

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
THE OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
It is again my pleasure to report on the activities of the Old Masonic Hall at Los
Angeles.
As in the years past, the Bethels of Jobs' Daughters, Order of Rainbow for
Girls and Masonic Lodges have all taken advantage of the privilege granted them
by holding meetings in our ancient Hall, and many letters from them attest to the
fact of their enjoyment in the use thereof. As in my last report, I can again say
that Loyalty Lodge No. 529 F. & A. M. has again been the first to reserve a
meeting for 1978 and Canoga Lodge No . 611 F. & A. M. was only a week
behind them.
Our Committee is hopeful that the article that appeared in our California
Freemason issue of September will call to the attention of other Lodges the
beauty and awe-inspiring feeling of reverence that meetings in our Hallowed
Halls impart to our Brethren. Those who have been fortunate enough to hold one
of their degree meetings there can ascertain to that feeling.
The Old Masonic Hall is open to visitors on Thursday, Friday and Saturday
from 10 A .M. to 3 P .M. and is available for the use of Masonic Lodge meetings
and affiliated group meetings at any time of day or evening, with the exception of
Thursday evenings when Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge meets.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

197

A close watch is made to control and reduce insurance premiums in face of
rising costs due to inflation. Premiums are tied to losses so the fewer the losses,
the lower the premium. A monthly report of all losses or claims is furnished to
the Grand Secretary and the Insurance Committee for analysis to endeavor to
control the causes of loss.
The Grand Master requested the Insurance Committee to conduct a study for
creation of a self-funding Fire Insurance Program for Temple properties as
p~oposed at the last Annual Communication in the Resolution entitled ''Temple
Fire Insurance Company'' which resolution was withdrawn pending development of sufficient facts to reach a decision.
After several conferences with the legal division of the Insurance
Commissioner's office of the State of California, it was determined that a
self- funding plan as proposed would be considered transaction of insurance and
would come under the laws of the State.
. To acco_mplish the objecti~e contemplated under the Resolution would require
mcorporat1on of a separate insurance company classified as "Reciprocal" or
"Inter-Insuran ce Exchange" and a certificate of authority must be secured
from the Insurance Commissioner.
In order to establish the necessary actuarial data upon which a decision must be
made, as to whether it is feasible for Grand Lodge to undertake such action, the
Gr~~ Secretary has s~nt. a questionnaire to each Temple Association requesting
stat1st1cal data for bmldmg values, insurance coverage, premiums and losses
sustained during the last ten years.
At this writing, about one-half of the Temple Associations have responded
and, therefore, our Committee does not have sufficient data as yet, upon which to
make a complete study or recommendation .
Respectfully submitted,
ELMER C. GUNTHER, Chairman

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

Your Insurance Committee continues to function in an advisory capacity to
assist the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master on matters relating to insurance
protection of property and legal liability of Grand Lodge and Constituent Lodges
and the responsibilities of their Officers.
The program in effect provides Broad Comprehensive insurance for physical
loss or damage to our properties in San Francisco, Decoto and Covina and also
includes our Constituent Lodges for legal liability for Bodily Injury or Property
Damage, Workers' Compensation insurance, loss or damage to personal property
and loss due to crime or dishonesty.
Our program is in step with the most sophisticated insurance coverages
available in the insurance marketplace and is supervised and administered by our
professional insurance advisers and has set a pattern which is now being followed
by almost all Grand Lodge Jurisdictions in other states.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC WIDOWS PROGRAM

REPORT OF SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON FISCAL AFFAIRS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
It is with a great deal of pride and humility that the Masonic Widows
Committee submits this report at the conclusion of its first year as a Grand Lodge
Special Committee.
Pride in this activity has resulted in repeatedly expressed words of appreciation
and happiness coming from the lips of emotionally affected wives of departed
Brothers. Humility is the constant companion of each Committee Representative
as a widow thanks the Master following a Lodge event, and asks to be assured of
an invitation to subsequent gatherings.
The support given to this project by the Grand Master and his Corps of Officers
has been reflected in the accelerated growth of the Program. This combined with
the dedication of the Committee members has been responsible for the achievement of hitherto unattained goals.
The Remembrance Certificate, which is an l.D. card given to the wives of
departed Brothers by their husband's Lodge, is now irx:luded in the scheduled
activities of seventy-one per cent of our Lodges-an irx:rease of fourteen per cent
over last year.
As refererx:e is made to participation in the Program it should be explained that
any form of Lodge recognition of these ladies qualifies the Lodge whether it be
social gatherings, personal contact, or phone conversation whereby the hand of
friendship and brotherly love is extended.
Throughout the entire Jurisdiction, in excess of eighty per cent of the Lodges
are participating in some form or another. This attention to the Widows, in
addition to bringing pleasure to them, is resulting in the reactivating of members
who had lost interest in attending meetings, and finarx:ial contributions from both
members and the ladies.
It has been the intent of the members of this Committee and a staff in excess of
one hundred and fifty members to assist the Lodges in inviting the Widows to
become part of our Masonic Family. With pride and humility we feel that our
efforts have been rewarded by the enthusiastic response of the Lodges throughout
the Jurisdiction.
We thank the Grand Master for the recognition he has given to this Committee,
and for the opportunity to have been of service to our Fraternity.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Advisory Committee on Fiscal Affairs exists to "furx:tion in an advisory
capacity to the Grand Master and to the Grand Lodge in regard to the fiscal affairs
of Grand Lodge."
In observance of this responsibility this Committee constantly monitors areas
of Grand Lodge fiscal affairs over and beyond the powers of the Grand Master
and the Grand Lodge itself. Our Grand Master has referred to this in his report to
Grand Lodge concerning "the multiplicity of government regulations both
Federal and State."
The Internal Revenue Code provides rules and regulations which the Grand
Lodge and its entities must observe in order to preserve the tax-exempt status we
enjoy.
The California Health Facilities Commission has provided regulations specifying the accounting and reporting system for California long term health facilities.
This is requiring extensive changes in the accounting records for the Masonic
Homes of California.
Both Congress and State Legislatures have committees considering requirements that the finarx:ial data of tax-exempt organizations shall be furnished in
uniform form in order to attain " full disclosure for the public right to know."
Partly as a result of these governmental developments the American Institute
of Certified Public Accounts is proposing an audit guide with a statement of
accounting prirx:iples and reporting practices applicable to nonprofit organizations. In time this work will have a major impact on the accounting practices
employed by Grand Lodge and its entities.
Your Committee on Fiscal Affairs concurs with the Grand Master's recommendation limiting changes by the exercise of executive powers. We remind the
Brethren that proper records and reports as required by the Federal and State
governments and other outside agerx:ies are not subject to our power to
modify-we must observe the law.
This Committee continues to make comprehensive reviews of the personnel in
the office of the Grand Secretary. From time to time, we obtain and analyze job
descriptions of all of the employees and examine the organization of the office.
We also make reviews of the salaries and fringe benefits and compare them to the
best available information or practices in the San Frarx:isco Bay Area.
There are, in addition to the Grand Secretary and the Assistant Grand
Secretary, some twenty-one employees of the Grand Lodge. It is necessary to
relate these employees to the activities required as to the administration and
accounting headquarters of four substantial corporations, a large pension fund,
and a charitable trust. It is also necessary to relate these employees to the
maintenance of some eighty million dollars of assets.
Your Committee is of the opinion that the work is present to require these
employees and that the Grand Secretary has a capable and devoted staff well able
to perform its arduous tasks.

REPORT OF
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
This is a new Committee, structured by Most Worshipful Kermit A. fa:obson,
Grand Master, for two purposes:
I . To assist Lodges suffering from loss of membership, poor attendance and
lack of Officers.
2 . To consult with "ailing Lodges," advise them and report to the Grand
Master.
The program would not have been possible were it not for the optimistic
viewpoint of the Grand Master. He has proclaimed throughout the Jurisdiction
that "Masonry is on the Move. " He has created an atmosphere favorable to the
work of the Committee.
Another factor in the ready a:x:eptance of the Committee has been the interest
and support of Very Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons, Grand Lecturer. Brother
Lemons has worked through the Ritual Committee to instill leadership qualities
in Lodge Officers and has made many appearances himself. His work has been
fruitful.
The Committee has made use of existing channels of communication and
extensive letter writing. Committee members have occasionally made personal
visits to Lodges with little or no expense to Grand Lodge.
Several printed helps to subordinate Lodges have been developed.
I. "Keeping Masonry on the Move" outlines a number of common sense
ideas to improve Lodge performance without making innovations in the body of
Masonry. The folder has been distributed to the Elective Lodge Officers.
2. "Information Kit" is a collection of several informational articles, some of
which have been available for years and some of which are new. It is instructive
to members and can be handed to a non-member who expresses an interest in
become a Mason.
3. "Check List for Lodge Officers" is a brief list of ideas and suggestions
distributed at the Annual Conference.
4. ' ' Basic Reader for Lodge Masters" is a conversational treatment of several
proven helps.

. This year our Masonic Temple celebrates its nineteenth birthday. Our Temple
is a landmark of Masonry, located at the top of Nob Hill here in San Francisco
and is. symbolic of the i~eals of Masonry. Each year adds to the beauty, elegance
of design and construction that not only we as Masons are justly proud of but the
City of San Francisco is also proud of having this beautiful Masonic Temple here
in the City by the ftay .
Our auditorium, because of its location and acoustical excellence, continues to
attrac~ n~w concerts, lectures and performances of musical plays. Business
orgamzauons, state governmental agencies and professional associations find our
Temple to be an excellent choice and most suitable to their various requirements
and needs for conducting successful meetings.
As !ruste~s of our Masonic Temple, we are charged with the responsibility of
o~ratmg ~h~s Temple as efficiently as possible to produce the greatest results
with a m1mmum of wasted effort and in a most effective manner that is
representative of our Great Fraternal Order. In order to maintain the beauty of our
Temple and prevent any deterioration, the Trustees found it necessary to do
considerable work on the exterior walls of the Temple. The south and west
exterior walls have been waterproofed to prevent any future damage that could
be caused by water and then repainted. All of the marble on the east and north walls
have been checked for defects and when necessary reset, caulked and then the
e~tire marble walls washed and cleaned from the very top of the Temple to the
sidewalk. All exterior metal surfaces were treated and repainted and concrete
surfaces waterproofed. A part of the sidewalk on the east side of the Temple was
replaced. These are the major renovation projects completed this year that will
add many years of life and beauty to this great edifice of Masonry.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Trustees call your attention to the work planned and completed by Grand
Lodge for Grand Lodge offices on the third floor of our Temple. This remodeling
produced a change that has brought a freshness of sunlight to what used to be a
crowded work space with wall to wall desks and typewriters.
Grand Lodge is most fortunate to have Brother George Gavin as the Executive
Vice-President and General Manager of this beautiful Temple. It is under his
direction and supervision with the assistance of Assistant Manager Loren M.
Stritenberger that the repairs and maintenance of the Temple are brought to
completion. Besides the major repairs and renovations to the Temple, constant
attention is given to the interior which requires constant effort on the part of our
Temple staff to maintain and preserve the beauty and utility of the Temple.
Membership in the San Francisco Convention and Visitors Bureau, Nob Hill
Association and greater San Francisco Chamber of Commerce has been continued and serve as a source of contacts from which many rental prospects are
obtained. Our rental income for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1977 has shown
an increase during the past year.
The Pine Street properties have been brought up to all city codes and justify the
maintenance expense of the buildings until a more appropriate use of the land can
be determined.
The Trustees are pleased to report that we have no outstanding indebtedness
unpaid except current operating expenses which are paid as incurred.
Thus, another Masonic year has come to a successful conclusion. Your
Trustees have endeavored to discharge their duties to the best of their ability that
this Masonic Temple will reflect to all who enter these portals the beauty, grace
and elegance of a truly great structure dedicated to serving the needs of our Great
Fraternity of Masons in the State of California.

California Lodges 1 to paid subscribers, and to other Grand Jurisdictions in the
United States and foreign countries.
The primary goal of the California Freemason is to keep the Masons of
California continually aware of the role Freemasonry plays in the cultural, social,
educational, and governmental process in state and nation.
The magazine serves as a link between Grand Lodge and those Masons who,
for many reasons, do not attend or participate as actively as they once did in their
Lodges.
Like most of the media, the California Freemason tries to appeal to the
different interests of its readers. Articles range from stories about early Masonic
history in California and the nation, through philosophic and moral dissertations
to the happenings in Constituent Lodges. Although of questionable cultural
value, over 1000 readers have participated in the puzzle contests during the past
year even though no prizes were offered.
In the last four issues more than 225 Lodge, District, and Grand Lodge events
were reported. Scholarships granted by the California Masonic Foundation,
Public Schools Week participation, Constitutional observances, and Masonic
Homes activities filled the pages.
During the past year readers were encouraged to send their opinions and ideas
to a new section of the magazine titled ''For the Good of the Order.'' While such
an invitation was a calculated risk and did elicit a certain number of letters to the
editor which began "Dear Sir, you cur," and others on controversial subjects, it
does provide members with one of the few open forums available for written
expression of beliefs and views.
The Publication Board requests that the annual per capita allocation of fifty
cents be continued during the ensuing year, making the cost of each issue to each
Mason in California less than that of a 13 cent stamp.
The editor is most appreciative of those members who contributed original
articles during tl?e past year, of the Officers and especially the Secretaries of the
Lodges for the submission of pictures and stories of Lodge events, and of the
patience and understanding of the Grand Scretary's office in handling the
increasing flow of mail which is the life blood of the California Freemason.

REPORT OF CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
"A respect for law and order, a respect for the Flag of the United States, for
the Constitution and laws by which we are governed, and, through the medium of
education, to teach young people of all classes and creeds that freedom under
law, as provided by our form of government, is a priceless heritage.''
These are the principles upon which the California Masonic Foundation was
founded on March 9, 1969 as a non-profit charitable corporation and an adjunct
of the Grand Lodge. Since that date, those who have been members of the Board
of Trustees over the years have endeavored in every way to live up to and carry
out those principles.
One way in which we have accomplished this is to assist in providing
educational opportunities for those deserving young people who need financial
assistance to attend college. Since 1969, we have awarded some 480 scholarships
and have expended some $321,000 in doing so. Many of those receiving these
awards have indicated that the funds so provided enabled them to continue and
complete their studies and receive their degrees where otherwise they would have
had to drop out.
Eligibility does not depend on Masonic relationships, but as above stated we
try to assist persons of every race or creed. Whenever an award is made through a
Masonic recommendation, however, we strongly urge that an award ceremony as
part of some Lodge event. of the recommending Lodge or member, be scheduled
and the award made by an Inspector or Lodge officer in the presence of the
recipient's friends and relatives.
Insofar as possible, all scholarships and all other charitable giving in which we
engage is distributed equally between Northern and Southern California, and we
assist Hawaiian De Mo lay. Hawaii also has representation on our Board of
Trustees.
I would be remiss if I failed to mention that a substantial amount of our funds
came to us from the Order of the Amaranth. This is a trust fund and its use is
strictly limited to females under 21 who are California residents. Approximately
one half of the above total awards have been made out of those funds, and we
wish to express our deep appreciation to all members of the Order of the
Amaranth, and to assure them that many young women have benefited from their
generosity.
Many persons, including Masters and Wardens, are still unaware that the
California Masonic Foundation exists as one of the Grand Lodge charitable
organizations. During the past year however, two letters have gone out to all
Inspectors, Masters, Wardens and Secretaries. One advises of our existence and
explains that funds are available for charitable purposes, that our principal
project is scholarship awards for needy students, and that the Foundation can
solicit and accept donations from the public for charitable purposes. The other
gives instructions for applying for a scholarship.
Our charitable giving is not limited to scholarships. During the last fiscal year,
the following amounts were granted to the following organizations or individuals:

211

The recommendation of the Committee on Policy and General Purpos~ on
1976 Resolution No. 14 is unchanged. We accordingly repeat our report of last
year:
This Resolution would establish the requirement that the Junior Warden, Senior
Warden and Master of a Lodge before being issued a Certificate of Proficiency
for the respective station shall have passed the Third Degree Proficiency by strict
examination in open Lodge.
At present the California Masonic Code (l 122-5th) requires the Inspector to
issue a certificate "to the Officers of the Lodges when they are qualified to give
the work and lectures required of them respectively, and are thoroughly proficient in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge
which relate to the government of the Lodge."
To be proficient in the work and lectures required of the Junior Warden, Senior
Warden and Master would certainly include a knowledge of Freemasonry such as
each Master Mason acquires on taking the proficiency in the Candidates' Lecture
of the Third Degree. To require more could cause undue hardship to many small
Lodges with few Officers and even to urban Lodges with difficulty obtaining
Officers.
The existing requirements properly emphasize the qualities necessary for the
leadership expected of Lodge Officers.
In addition, the Officers · nominated are elected by the votes of the Brethren
of their Lodges. The Brethren can be expected to exercise their suffrage with due
concern for the selection of proper leadership.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
Adopted.

.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
(1976-Resolution No. 17)
Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The Comminee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Resolution concerning modification of our present requirements respecting physical qualifications to receive the Degrees of Masonry has been carried
over from the 1976 Annual Communication for decision at this Communication.
In the past decade particularly, the issue contained in this proposal has been
debated, and debated, and debated. Proponents and opponents are zealously
sincere in their respective positions.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes feels there is nothing to be
gained by exhaustive and exhausting continuation of the debate, and we heartily
endorse the Grand Master's determination to limit presentation on this matter to
no more than twelve minutes.
Irrespective of one's feelings or convictions concerning physical qualifications
themselves, there is one part of the proposal which deserves special consideration. The last sentence of the proposed new Section 2603 outlining the manner of

ADOPT LANDMARKS RECITED BY MACKEY
(1)
To the Most Worshipfu.l Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Article III of the California Masonic Code declares the Grand
Lodge of California to be obedient to THE FOUNDATION OF MASONIC
LAW; viz: The Ancient Landmarks or Unwritten Law; and
WHEREAS, by precedent the Grand Lodge has referred to The Ancient
Landmarks as recorded by Mackey and published the same on numerous
occasion (CMC, First Edition, 1956; et alii); and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge has not formally adopted the Foundation of
Masonic Law, the Ancient Landmarks; and
WHEREAS, every Master Mason is CHARGED as follows: "Our Ancient
Landmarks you are carefully to preserve, and never suffer them, on any pretense,
to be infringed;" and
WHEREAS, it having been customary among Masons of many areas, since
time immemorial, to Communicate "in another manner" instruction relative to
unwritten Masonic Law; vis: THE FOUNDATION OF MASONIC LAW; and
WHEREAS, said Communication should be delivered to each and every
Mason .at an early date subsequent to his receiving the Masters Degree; and
WHEREAS, it is common knowledge within Lodges that Communication of
our Ancient Landmarks is not being achieved; nor is there any specific and
proper method provided to accomplish the same, thereby in effect denying this
vital intelligence to many Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, the very lack of knowledge and understanding of our Ancient
Landmarks may and can lead to the compromise of the credibility of the Ancient
Landmarks.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Grand Lodge of California formally adopt the Ancient Landmarks, as recited by Mackey, to be The
Foundation of Masonic Law; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Grand Lodge of California amend
Article I of its Ordinance with the following addition to Paragraph 1114 (duties
of the Grand Lecturer):

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

217

7th. To devise and institute a proper time and method designed to Communicate The Ancient Landmarks to each and every Mason who has achieved the
Masters Degree.
Respectfully submitted,
W. G. BURRIS, PM No. 12
Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes
and on Ritual.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. I proposes that Mackey's statement of the Ancient Landmarks
be adopted by this Grand Lodge and that the Grand Lecturer devise a means of
communicating them to each Master Mason.
Our Masonic concept of landmarks comes from the Bible.
We read in Proverbs 22:28, "Remove not the ancient landmark which thy
fathers have set." In Deuteronomy 27:17 there is written "Cursed be he that
removeth his neighbour's landmark.''
Thus in the sense of something immovable and unchangeable do we as
Freemasons view the Landmarks. Perhaps even more Landmarks are regarded as
part of the unwritten law or tenets and thus as traditions or things fundamental,
handed down from time immemorial, which the great majority agree cannot be
changed.
Mackey's 25 Landmarks have been adopted by 12 Grand Lodges in the United
States, but other lists ranging from 7 to 54 in number have been adopted by 14
Grand Lodges. 13 Grand Lodges have not adopted any list.
If a Landmark.exists from time immemorial, it should require no affirmation
now. If it were to be adopted by this Grand Lodge, that action would suggest that
the Landmark can be changed or repealed by Grand Lodge, in which event it
would not be a genuine Landmark.
It is as unnecessary to adopt an official list of Landmarks as to adopt an official
list of scientific laws, such as the law of gravity. The Landmarks, like scientific
laws, are valid only insofar as they are true.
Believing unanimously that it is unnecessary to adopt Landmarks, your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Resolution No. I has been referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which
reports as follows:
This Resolution seeks to have the Grand Lodge formally adopt the Ancient
Landmarks of the Order, as recited by Mackey, to be the Foundation of Masonic
Law, and to add to the duties of the Grand Lecturer the duty to provide for
communication of them to every Brother who achieves the degree of Master
Mason.
To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following:

RESOLVED FURTHER, that Section 1114 of the California Masonic Code
be amended by adding the following:
7th. To devise and institute a proper time and method designated to communicate the Ancient Landmarks to each and every Mason who has achieved the

The Committee on Ritual:
As proposed by Resolution No. 1 we would be adopting Mackey's Landmarks
in their entirety. My Brethren, the adoption of the aforementioned Landmarks
would place us in direct conflict with some of our present laws.
Our present mode of operation, of adhering to those Ancient Landmarks by
custom, has proven to be an excellent guide.
It is the opinion of this Committee that the adoption of Mackey's Landmarks
would not improve the communication of the same.
After some research it has been found that most of the Grand Lodges have
found the ideal situation is to use either their own list or none. In fact, 27 Grand
Lodges so operate. There are only 12 Grand Lodges who have adopted Mackey's
Landmarks. As a matter of record, some of the Grand Lodges who had adopted
Mackey's Landmarks have made innovations thereto.
Your Ritual Committee recommends the adoption of the motion, but further
recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

RECITE TWENTY-FIVE LANDMARKS
IN C.M.C. SUPPLEMENTS
(lA)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the recognition of immutable laws relating to the Masonic
Institution, which the Fraternity itself cannot change and remain Masonic in
character, imposes upon the governing bodies the DUTY of seeing that "The
Ancient Landmarks be preserved;'' and
WHEREAS this DUTY has, since time immemorial, introduced into the
Masonic system of jurisprudence a feature peculiar to itself; viz: the recognition,
perpetuation and obedience to these unwritten laws of antiquity that are unrepealable; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge of California has, since inception, recognized
these Ancient Landmarks as unwritten voluntary, customary, conventional and

219

"ARTICLE III, POWERS OF GRAND LODGE, Paragraph 100
POWERS IN GENERAL. The Grand Lodge is the Supreme Masonic Power
and Authority in this Jurisdiction and is vested with all legislative, executive, and
judicial powers, LIMITED ONLY BY A STRICT ADHERENCE TO THE
ANCIENT LANDMARKS OF THE ORDER, and by the provisions of its own
Constitution and Regulations.''
And furthermore Annotation lOOd-4 requires that any grand body seeking
recognition as a sovereign Grand Lodge must recognize and support the Ancient
Landmarks; and
WHEREAS, the unwritten Ancient Landmarks have been reduced to writing
in brief form by recognized Masonic scholars and recited in CMC, First Edition,
1956 at pages 342 and 343; and
WHEREAS, the brief recitations referred to in the paragraph next above have
been omitted from the newly published editions of the California Masonic Code
thereby denying THE FOUNDATION OF MASONIC LAW its rightful place
within our written Masonic Code and furthermore denying the Craft easy access
to these writings that are necessary for basic understanding of The Ancient
Landmarks.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that all future printed supplements
and editions of the California Masonic Code shall recite therein in written form,
containing no written explanations, hypotheses, appendices or judgments, as
follows:
THE FOUNDATION OF MASONIC LAW
THE LANDMARKS, OR UNWRITTEN LAW
and further recite thereunder the twenty-five Landmarks exactly as recited in
CMC, First Edition, 1956, at pages 342 and 343.
Respectfully submitted,
W. G. BURRIS, PM No. 12
Referred to Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution requires that all future supplements and editions of the
California Masonic Code contain Mackey's 25 Landmarks.
There is presented in this jurisdiction "on the date of his raising to the sublime
degree of Master Mason as a souvenir of Brotherly regard from the members of
the Lodge" a copy of the Constitution and By-Laws. Page 21 of this booklet lists
the Landmarks or the unwritten Law. This is provided to every Master Mason
and we believe gives adequate exposure.

BRETHREN WHO MAY ATTEND
THE ANNUAL ELECTION

(2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Article IV Section 158 of the Constitution of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California states:
"BRETHREN WHO MAY ATTEND. Except during elections any Master
Mason who is a member of a Constituent Lodge in this Grand Lodge or other
recognized Grand Lodges may be present during an Annual or Special
Communication. Only members of this Grand Lodge and recognized representatives of other Grand Lodges may be present during election," and
WHEREAS, numerous Master Masons who are not members of this Grand
Lodge attend the Annual Communication each year, particularly on the final day
in order to witness the impressive ceremony of the installation of the Grand
Lodge Officers, and
WHEREAS, under the present constitution, such Master Masons must be
denied admission to the Grand Lodge on the final day until called off for the open
installation of Officers, arid
WHEREAS, the refusal to permit such Master Masons to enter the Grand
Lodge at that time causes great disappointment and many hard feelings each
year, and
WHEREAS, such Master Masons could be seated in the balcony during the
election of Officers without interference just as they are during the deliberations
.
on resolutions on the preceeding day,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Article IV Section 158 of the
Constitution of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of California be amended to read as follows:
"BRETHREN WHO MAY ATTEND. Any Master Mason who is a member
of a Constituent Lodge in this Grand Lodge or other recognized Grand Lodges
may be present during an Annual or Special Communication."
Respectfully submitted,
M. WILLIAM HOLSINGER, PM No. 259
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

221

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 2 proposes to amend Section 158 of the C.M.C. to delete the
prohibition that Master Masons who are not members of this Grand Lodge may
not attend elections at Annual or Special Communications of Grand Lodge.
This Resolution would permit any Master Mason to attend all sessions of any
Annual or Special Communication.
Because it would cause no significant problems with balloting as such Master
Masons could be seated in the balcony during elections, and because attendance
at elections would generate and promote interest in and good feeling toward the
Grand Lodge procedures among such Master Masons, your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes believes that this legislation would be beneficial to our
Institution.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Committee On Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated that the language submitted by the
proponent would accomplish the purpose of the Resolution.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

(5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M: of California:
WHEREAS, the present method as adopted by the Grand Lodge at t.he Annual
Communication of 1974, does not provide for a wider representation of the
members of Grand Lodge to have a voice in the selection of the "recommendee"
for the office of Junior Grand Warden, and
WHEREAS the Elective Grand Line is charged with the responsibility and
operation of th~ Grand Lodge, it is felt that they, in the pursuance of their duties
in traveling throughout this Grand Jurisdiction and m~e~ing with the Maste~s and
Wardens of the Constituent Lodges, are in a better position to meet, ascertam and
evaluate the qualifications of an individual for the office of Junior Grand
Warden, and

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

223

WHEREAS, the Past Grand Masters are not charged with this responsibility
and operation of the Grand Lodge and are not required to travel as are the Elected
Grand Officers and therefore do not meet with as many members of the
Constituent Lodges and members of the Grand Lodge as they did while in office,
and
WHEREAS, it is the consensus of many that the system as employed now
should be changed to better representation of those responsible for the charge and
care of the Grand Lodge and therefore the better to promote harmony among the
Brethren of this Grand Jurisdiction,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Article V Sect. 200 be
amended as follows: The committee for the selection of a "recommendee" for
the office of Junior Grand Warden shall be composed of the Grand Master, the
Deputy Grand Master, the Grand Wardens, the Grand Lecturer, three Wardens
(Senior or Junior), from the Constituent Lodges, two from the South and one
from the North when the selectee is from the South, and two from the North and
one from the South when the selectee is from the North-to alternate each year,
and three Past Grand Masters, who are not present elective Grand Lodge
Officers, two from the South and one from the North when the selectee is from
the South, and two from the North and one from the South when the selectee is
from the North-to alternate each year, making a total of eleven members. The
members of this committee shall be appointed annually by the Grand Master, to
serve a single term only and concurrently with the term of the appointing Grand
Master. The Grand Master shall be the chairman of the committee. This
committee to evaluate the qualifications of a "recommendee" for the office of
Junior Grand Warden, and may receive· and consider recommendations from the
members of this Grand Lodge of those fully qualified for the office of Junior
Grand Warden.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the recommendee alternately shall be a
member of a Lodge in the North and of a Lodge in the South. The name of the
recommendee and his biographical sketch shall be sent to each Inspector and
Master of each Lodge, and may be sent to such other members of the Grand
Lodge as the Grand Master may direct, within 30 days following the selection by
the Recommending Committee but in no case later than 90 days prior to the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. All dissemination of the information thereafter shall be oral and not by any other means of reproduction. It is
expected that the information shall be communicated promptly and as often as
necessary by the Inspectors and the Masters and through them to other members
of the Grand Lodge in their respective Lodges. Also, it shall be further
understood that proper nominations may be made from the floor on the day of
election.
Respectfully submitted,
MILTON E. AMMANN, PM No. 600

225

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolutions regarding election procedures for a Junior Grand Warden have
been presented at Grand Lodge Annual Communications of 1972, 1974 and
1977. Except for relatively minor exceptions or refinements, there are striking
similarities in these resolutions.
In his annual message at the 1972 Communication, Grand Master McElwain
recommended that a study be made to consider all phases of the subject of the
election of a Junior Grand Warden. As a result of that recommendation the
resolution presented in 1972 was withdrawn.
The study was completed and a report with a recommendation was submitted
at the 1973 Communication. The ballot on the recommendation, although
favorable did not receive a 5/6 majority and so was held over to the 1974
Communication at which time it was adopted.
Thus, at the 1974 Communication, the members of Grand Lodge adopted a
formal written policy relating to the selection of a Junior Grand Warden
recommendee including a method for communicating information regarding that
selection to members of the Grand Lodge. The new procedure constituted a
committee of all of the Past Grand Masters together with three members of Grand
Lodge appointed annually by the Grand Master. That this system has worked
well is evidenced in the persons of the Grand Wardens present here. Reports
coming to us indicate that the information regarding the selectee has been
disseminated more thoroughly than before adoption of this formal policy.
The proponent of Resolution No. 5 states that since the Elective Grand Line is
charged with the operation of Grand Lodge (therefore travelling throughout the
Jurisdiction) they are in a better position to select a recommendee for Junior
Grand Warden than are the Past Grand Masters. He further states that the Past
Grand Masters do not operate Grand Lodge, do not travel and therefore do not
have the opportunity to meet as many members of Grand Lodge as they did while
in office.
These statements overlook the function performed by the three members of
Grand Lodge appointed to the selection committee each year by the Grand
Master. These annual appointees come to the committee meetings without
constraint of any sort and bring to the selection committee names of potential
recommendees from the geographical areas in which they are familiar and
knowledgeable.
These statements also overlook the fact that the Past Grand Masters represent
wide geographical areas and are well acquainted with Masonic activities and
outstanding Masons in those areas. They attend many Masonic functions in their
respective areas and it is at these functions that outstanding men of unusual
ability are noticed by them. In the due course of events the Past Grand Masters
may well observe the development of abilities in these men over periods of time
as long as, or longer than, the four years of service of the Elected Grand Line. It
should also be noted that the Past Grand Masters are always receptive to
suggestions from every source as to men of outstanding potential who may one
day warrant recognition in some higher Masonic office.
Further, the Past Grand Masters have experienced the duties of all of the
offices of the progressive elected line and are in a position to judge all factors in
regard to a potential recommendee.

As we stated earlier, the system has worked well, not only as modified in 197 4
but for many, many years in the history of this Grand Lodge. Capable and
dedicated men have served the Grand Lodge of California which is recognized as
one of the outstanding Grand Jurisdictions in all of Freemasonry.
Resolution No. 5 would direct the Grand Master to send the biographical
sketch of the recommendee to the Master of each Lodge (as well as to each
Inspector). Although the Grand Master is not required by current law to send a
sketch to any other than Inspectors (other mailings optional), we find that in the
three years of operating under the current procedure, Grand Masters, in fact,
have included in the original mailing the Masters of each Lodge, Inspectors,
Grand Lodge officers, Past Grand Masters, members of Grand Lodge Committees, Homes Board of Trustees, Temple Board-an even more complete list than
Resolution No. 5 proposes.
Resolution No. 5 also would permit nominations from the floor of Grand
Lodge.
Such procedure inherently would be dangerous to the peace and harmony of
Freemasonry in this Grand Jurisdiction.
Aside from lack of information as to ability, willingness to serve, proper
geographical location, etc., in regard to a member nominated from the floor, of
even more concern to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is the
question of electioneering.
A few of our sister Grand Jurisdictions permit electioneering and those who
have had an opportunity to observe those processes are grateful for our law and
tradition. We are confident that you would not like to see campaign headquarters
set up in hotel suites with the possibility of elaborate cocktail parties and
promotional giveaways-all of which, in the opinion of the Committee, detract
from and tarnish the high office to which some member will be elected. It is
entirely possible that the individual thus elected could be the member who could
afford to spend the most in seeking office-a prospect which is contrary to
lessons taught in our Degrees.
Electioneering, either for Masonic office or to influence the votes of members
of Grand Lodge as to legislation to come before that body has been considered a
most reprehensible evil throughout the history of our Grand Lodge. The proceedings of 1868, 1893 and 1904 contain examples of this particular subject coming
openly to the attention of the members of our Grand Lodge. In 1893 this Grand
Lodge again had approved legislation prohibiting electioneering and sought
further to determine just what in the strong hand of penal statutes should be
legislated so as to discipline violators of the basic Masonic prohibition against
electioneering.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes most strongly believes that
the cause of Masonry in California is best served by maintaining all prohibitions
against electioneering and we unamimously urge you to vote "No" on this
resolution.

224

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence submitted language and moved its adoption
without recommendation.
Not Adopted.

RITUAL SCHOOLS OF INSTRUCT IONLIMITING MANDATORY ATTENDANCE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 8 proposes to excuse from mandatory attendance at schools of
instruction those Officers of a Lodge not generally scheduled for advancement
through the chairs of that Lodge.
While the Policy and General Purposes Committee agrees that it is not always
essential for certain Officers to attend schools of instruction in ritual, Section
1122, 3rd of the C.M.C. relates also to instruction in matters relating to
government of the Lodge and proper administration of its affairs and other
matters for the welfare of the Craft. Such instruction may be of considerable
bene?t t~ Secretaries and Treasurers, for example. Further, if the purpose of the
meeting is unrelated to the duties of any Officer, this fact should be reasonable
cause for non-attendance and obviously can be reasonably administered by the
Inspectors.
I move adoption of Resolution No. 8 and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

Resolution No. 8 proposes to change Section I 122-3rd of the C.M.C. to limit
