W~at is a line officer in accordance with the proponents' resolution? A good
question. The answer may be quite varied between Lodges,-even between
Lodges in the. same District. One Lodge may start the so-called line at the Senior
Deacon's station, another at the Junior Deacon, still others at the Stewards'
and/or the Marshal's station. The time in the line could be from as short as 3
years to as long as 8 years.
~ile the preamble to this Resolution states that "very little, if any, instruction has been provided for Lodge Secretaries, Treasurers, Organists, and other
non-line Officers at such meetings" we believe that such is not the case. The
named Offic~rs participate in the floor work at the opening of all Lodges and in
the first section of the Entered Apprentice Degree, and the Secretary has a

major role in the second section of the Third Degree, while the other non-line

Officers' Associations tbe so-called non-line Officers who perform in every

Section 1122-lst states that "it shall be the duty of the Inspector to hold
Schools of Instruction and instruct the Officers of the Lodges in the ritual.'' My
Brethren, Officers in this section is plural and means all Officers and not just
those who aspire to the Master's chair via the so-called line.
Such is our law to date. To change it to require the attendance of the so-called
line Officers only would, we believe, seriously undermine the excellence of our
California Ritual.
While a goodly number of the Treasurers, Secretaries and Organists in our
Lodges are dedicated Past Masters, we do not believe that the other non-line
Officers chairs are filled by them. We believe that each one of us who are doing
the Ritual, Assistant Grand Lecturers, Inspectors and Officers of the Lodges, be
they Past Masters or not, benefit from refreshment courses.
We therefore recommend no change in our law as to the mandatory attendance
at the meetings of the Officers' Associations but we do recommend to the
Inspectors that they excuse the Treasurer, Secretary, Organist and Tiler from all
schools, but are most welcome to attend.

performance of their duties. This amendment would replace the present system of
reimbursement of actual expenses for these particular items.
While there exist viable arguments that this change would simplify the system
of reimbursement of these expenses, and as a result thereof would relieve all
parties concerned, including the Grand Secretary and the Finance Committee, of
certain burdens, it appears to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that this legislation would not be beneficial to our Fraternity for the following
reasons:
1. An "amount per diem" is an allowance rather than a direct reimbursement,
and such practice compounds problems of verification of required attendance and
by its very nature, causes the maximum expense allowable to become the
minimum expense incurred;
2. There are presently in existence Instructions and Regulations pertaining to
expense claims for Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors, and members of Boards
and Committees. These regulations, promulgated following a Report of Special
Finance Study Committee which was read and adopted in principle at the 1968
Grand Lodge Communication, are the product of a thorough and exhaustive
review of the subject. These established standards for reimbursement provide a
clear definition of reimbursable expenses for food and lodging and a workable
method for claiming such proper reimbursement. To discard the present system
in favor of an imprecise per diem system would be irresponsible.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

232

233

2. The present requirement of receipts is a proper procedure from an accounting standpoint. It is safe under any scrutiny by any audit for both the Grand
Lodge and the individual involved.
3. It is well known that most, if not all, of the Grand Lodge Officers,
Inspectors and Committeemen spend some of their own funds and do not request
reimbursement. For those approved expenses, proper receipts will enable the
individual to be more fairly reimbursed than a per diem allowance which by
necessity may be an amount lower than the actual expense.

Lodge Officers would review the receipts attached to Expense Reimbursement
Requests and thus be better able to plan and stay within assigned budgets.
5. Your Finance Committee is comprised of men familiar with good accounting principles who cannot condone anything but good accounting practices and
expense control.

PROVIDE FOR TRANSACTION OF BUSINESS WHEN

The Committee on Ritual:
The Committee on Ritual to which was referred Resolution No. 11, reports as
follows:
This Resolution proposes to reduce from 7 members present to only 3 in order
to transact the business of a Lodge.
To effect this change would require revamping of the entire ritualistic
procedllre and language pertaining to the opening of a Lodge of Master Masons
since it would be both verbally and physically impossible with only 3 members
present to use the current ritual. Any changes in ritual must necessarily be
approved by Grand Lodge itself.
Beyond the mere matter of ritual, it would appear to this Committee that even
a small. Lodge which could not "field" 7 members, including Officers, to attend
a Stated Meeting and use the current ritual procedure-even in extenuating
circumstances- is in need of rejuvenation beyond that of which a change of
ritual could provide.
·
We urge a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

It is difficult to perceive any way in which moderation in the use of champagne
could be controlled and assured , and the reference to "strict supervision by
Grand Lodge or Lodges' Temple Manager" to prevent excess appears to the
Committee to be unreasonably optimistic.
Each of us has been charged upon becoming a Master Mason to "preserve
unsullied the reputation of the Fraternity.'' By providing Masonic facilities for
non-Masonic events at which the effect of intoxicants might lead to some of those
in attendance to becoming noisy or unruly could result in the conclusion in the
minds of neighboring residents or passers-by that Masons did not entirely
observe the limits of good conduct. We believe that in accordance with decorum
and propriety, there is never any reason why any beverage with alcoholic
content, including champagne, should be served in Masonic Temples.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote .

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, many Masonic Lodges own or lease buildings with Lodge Room
and adjacent social hall and cooking facilities and are in need of financial
assistance from rental revenues;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that, provided the Lodge Room is
separate from the social hall and facilities and has a separate entrance: . such
Lodges may rent their social hall and facilities for weddings, banquets, socials,
and other legalized activities, and the lessee may be allowed to serve champagne
with food through a caterer under strict supervision of Grand Lodge or Lodges'
Temple Manager; provided that no individual or entity having control of said
building may become a licensee for the purpose of serving alcoholic beverages,
and further provided, that no alcoholic beverages may be sold, served or
consumed during the time the Masonic Lodge or any affiliated youth groups are
in session.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that, a sign posted be displayed stating that
this is not a Masonic activity.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 12 again seeks permission of Grand Lodge for a Lodge to serve
champagne in its social hall.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is in sympathy with the search
by Lodges for additional revenues. Those Lodges having investment in owned or
leased buildings wherein facilities sufficiently separated from the Lodge Room
may be rented for weddings, banquets, socials and other legalized activities seek
authority to permit renters to serve champagne with food through a caterer at
such events.

"Section 2051. SERVING CHAMPAGNE IN SOCIAL HALL.
If the room used for ·stated or Degree Meetings by a Masonic Lodge or a
prerequisite organization has a separate entrance and is separated from and, by
closing its doors, can be isolated from other rooms used for social purposes, then
such rooms used for social purposes, and not a part of the Lodge room area, may
be rented for weddings, banquets, social benefits and other activities approved by
the Grand Lodge, and the tenant may be permitted to serve champagne with food
through a duly licensed caterer, under the supervision of the Grand Lodge or the
Lodge Temple Manager, and a sign must be displayed stating that the affair is not
a Masonic acitivity; provided that no individual or entity having control of the
building or any part thereof may be or become a licensee for the purpose of
serving alcoholic beverages within the building; and further provided that no
such beverage may be sold, served or consumed during the time a Masonic
Lodge, prerequisite organization or any youth group is holding a meeting in the
building."
To place this matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of this
Resolution.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Commitee on Temple Properties:
This resolution is premised on the basis that many Lodges are in need of
financial assistance and may obtain that assistance by renting the social hall and
cooking facilities on the following terms and conditions:
1. The Lodge Room must be separate from the social hall and facilities to be
rented and have a separate entrance.
2. The social hall and facilities may be rented for weddings, banquets, socials
and other legalized activities.
3. Champagne may be served if food is served through a caterer .
4 . Grand Lodge or the Temple Manager must strictly supervise.
5. No individual or entity having control of said building may become a
licensee for the purpose of serving alcoholic beverages.
6. No alcoholic beverages may be sold, served or consum~ during the time
the Masonic Lodge or any affiliated youth groups are in session.
No doubt the renting of its social hall can be a help financially to a Lodge.
If we concur that champagne may be served in the Lodge's social hall for
specified events the Resolution is uncertain in the following:
1. Does the phrase "separate entrance" refer to the building or the Lodge
Room itself?
2. If champagne only is to be served at a wedding it seems unlikely that any
kind of license would be required, yet the resolution refers to a license and twice
to alcoholic beverages. Alcoholic beverages is a broader term than champagne
and its use here seems to imply that more than champagne may be involved.
3. The term "and other legalized activities" seems to mean activities that
were once illegal and have now been made legal. Does it refer to Masonic law or
to California and Hawaiian law?
4. Strict supervision of a social event in an individual Temple building by
Grand Lodge seems impossible. Maybe it means that Grand Lodge is to adopt
further rules and regulations concerning such activities before the Resolution
becomes effective.
5. The phrase "no individual or entity having control of said building may
become licensee" would literally prohibit a Lodge or Temple Association from
holding a liquor license. I would believe this is presently the law. It may refer to
the one who rents the social hall for the social event and prohibits that person
from being the holder of an alcoholic beverage license. Again it may be an
attempt to assure the Lodge that the renter will use the premises for a purpose that
will not require a liquor license .
6. Since the use of champagne only is a somewhat limited use, is it realistic to
believe the Resolution would help a Lodge in attracting banquets, socials and
other "legalized activities?"
In summary, whether the intent is to allow only champagne be served or
something more, the whole Resolution should be redone to clarify the intent and
limitations.
The Committee moves the adoption of the Resolution and recommends a
"'No" vote.
Not Adopted.

news bulletins or programs, and that such advertising shall be subject to rules and
regulations of the Committee on Commercialism of this Grand Lodge.
Parenthetically, mention should be made that the proponents incorrectly
suggest amendment of Section 334, which was the applicable section number
regulating advertising and publication in the former California Masonic Code; in
the present California Masonic Code the section number involved is Section
2072. Also, it should be pointed out that at the 1976 Communication of this
Grand Lodge, Resolution No. l l contained in part a somewhat similar proposal
affecting the prohibition against advertising in Trestleboards and monthly news
bulletins, but the proponents of the 1976 Resolution No. l l suggested and
consented to the deletion from such Resolution No. 11 that portion thereof
relating to Masonic Trestleboards and news bulletins. Consequently, the legislation ultimately enacted at the 1976 Communication, growing out of Resolution
No. 11, did not affect Masonic Trestleboards or Masonic news bulletins but
amended Section 2072 only as to restricted printing permitted under specified
conditions in certain charity football game programs only where sponsored by
organizations requiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite for membership
therein.
To carry out the intent of the proponents of Resolution No. 14, it becomes
necessary to: (a)amend the first paragraph of Section 2072 of the California
Masonic Code; (b) place an appropriate note after Annotations 2072a and 2072b;
and (c) amend the first and second paragraph of the Section entitled "I.
Advertising'' of the Regulations Governing Organizations subject to the Jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California contained in
the Appendix of the California Masonic Code.
Your Committee therefore submits the following legislation:
RESOLVED that the first paragraph of Section 2072 of the California Masonic
Code be amended to read as follows:
"No Lodge, or member of a Lodge, shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print
advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication, which purports to
be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body,
order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership, except that there may be printed in Masonic or Masonic related
Trestleboards, monthly news bulletins and programs, and in charity football

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

239

programs only sponsored by organizations requiring Masonic membership
therein, when the proceeds of the game go to a Masonic or Masonic related
charity, complimentary advertisements, such as 'Compliments of _ _ ' or
'Best wishes from _ _ , with name of individuals or companies inserted in
the blanks, but not naming any product as such, and provided that the proceeds
from such advertisements shall not exceed the cost of printing and mailing or
distributing such Trestleboards, monthly news bulletins or programs and that
such advertising shall be subject to rules and regulations of the Committee on
Commercialism of this Grand Lodge".
RESOLVED FURTHER that, immediately following Annotations 2072a and

RESOLVED ALSO that in California Masonic Code, in the Appendix thereof,

~ad twenty or more applications for membership at a Stated Meeting, requiring

"Provided, however, that the provisions of Section 2086 and 2638 of this

SYDNEY ZAID, PM No. 415
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 15 proposes to permit Research Lodges to receive applications
for membership without the requirement of referral to a committee of three for
investigation and a report thereon.
This matter was last presented at the 1969 Annual Communication as Resolution No. 23, and was not adopted.
It should be noted that there is a basic difference between Research Lodges and
other Lodges.
Section 2124 of the California Masonic Code states: "Research Lodges. A
special classification of constituent Lodges is hereby established, to be known as
Research Lodges, with authority to conduct research, hold discussion, gather and
preserve Masonic information, maintain a library, supply papers or speakers at
the request of other Lodges when convenient, and conduct a program of general
service to the Craft in the field of Masonic Education and Information_''
A Research Lodge has no power to confer Degrees.
A Research Lodge is not liable for any relief.
A Research Lodge is not entitled to representation in the Grand Lodge nor any
vote therein.
A Research Lodge is exempt from contributions levied upon Lodges.
No officer is, by reason of that position alone, a member of Grand Lodge.
A Master of a Research Lodge cannot become or be known as or designated as
a Past Master.
A Research Lodge has no judicial power. Suspension of a member of a
Research Lodge for non-payment of dues does not affect his membership in any
other Lodge.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
Resolution No. 15 proposes to eliminate the requirement for referral of
application for memberships in Research Lodges to a committee for investigation
and report thereon.
The proponent has consented and concurs with an amendment to the proposed
resolution that changes the time that the application for membership is voted on
from the meeting at which the application is submitted and read to the following
Stated Meeting.
To carry out the intent of the proponent, your Committee submits the
following:
RESOLVED, that Section 2124, subparagraph 12, of the California Masonic
Code be amended by adding the following at the end thereof:
"provided, however, that the provisions of Sections 2086 and 2638 of this
Code for referral of applications to a committee of three for investigation and
report thereon shall not apply to Research Lodges and that applications for
membership may be voted on at the Stated Meeting following the meeting at
which they are submitted and read."
To place this matter before Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of this
resolution.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

investigation is required.''

RECOGNITION OF VETERAN MASTER MASONS60 AND 70 YEARS
(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, at the present time there is no recognition given to qualified
California Masons by the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California for those
Brothers who have reached sixty (60) and seventy (70) years as a Mason;
WHEREAS, this is a milestone that few of us will ever reach, and is one that
should be celebrated as well as the fifty and seventy-five year recognitions;
WHEREAS, at the present time it is known that other Grand Lodges do
recognize these milestones and make every effort to celebrate the occasion;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that C.M.C. 2436 be amended by
adding 2436B to read as follows:
"In addition to the fifty and seventy-five year buttons, the Grand Lodge, upon
request, shall provide a gold sixty (60) year button to members of this
Jurisdiction who have been in good standing for sixty (60) years or more. The
provision of this section shall also apply in respect to a request for issuance of
a seventy (70) year button.

Respectfully submitted,
L. CLARK HANNA, PM No. 741
WILLIAM A. MORRE, M No. 741
M. DAVID MAC CAlLUM, SW No. 741 JESSE c. NEWMAN, JW No. 741
ROY c. ROBERTSON, PM No. 741
CLARENCE E. GREY , PM No. 741
WADE BURCHELL, PM No. 741
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and on
Finance.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 2436 of the C.M.C. provides for recognition of Veteran Master
Masons for 50 and 75 years of membership in good standing.
Resolution No. 17 would amend this section to include recognition for the 60th
and 70th years.
We are all proud to be Masons. The length of the term of our membership is
testimony to our continuing belief in the Fraternity, its precepts and principles.
So even the yearly anniversary of a Master Mason's membership in good
standing is an event. After 25 years of membership, some individual Lodges
make recognition of this fact with an appropriate ceremony.
Memberships which evidence the beliefs of the Fraternity are meaningful
accomplishments. Longevity alone is not determinative. However, to achieve 50
years as a Master Mason is truly an exceptional accomplishment for which the
Grand Lodge in its wisdom has elected to present in ceremony the gold 50-year
Veteran's Award Button.
To now add a 60 and 70-year award would stress longevity alone. The desired
affect is a singular award to be made after 50 years of membership in good
standing. This cherished emblem with its attending impressive ceremony would
be diluted and detracted from by adding further awards. Of course, the few and
rare 75-year awards notwithstanding would be even more tarnished by numerous
awards over the years.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
Resolution No. 17 has been referred to your Committee on Grand Lodge
Finance, and we applaud its intent. However, your Finance Committee must cast
. a hard, fiscally responsible eye upon any proposal which would involve the
expenditure of additional Grand Lodge funds, especially at a time when we are
beginning the second consecutive year in which budgeted expenses will exceed
projected income. If history is any guide, actual expense will, in all probability,
again exceed even the budgeted amount. We must ask ourselves whether the
benefits which will accrue to Masonry as a result of the presentation of the
limited number of these proposed recognition buttons will justify the considerable expense which will be incurred.
Your Finance Committee does not feel that these benefits will accruewhatever its other virtues undeniably are-and must, therefore, recommend a
"No" vote on Resolution No. 17.
Not Adopted.

VETERANS' AWARDS-TIME CREDIT

(18)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the 50-year Veteran Button is a cherished emblem that both
advertises the good will of our Fraternity, and encourages Brethren to continue
their membership in our Lodges, and
WHEREAS, many Brethren, through suspension for non-payment of dues due
to inability to pay tend to lose precious "service time" in the records of the
Grand Lodge, although in their hearts, they never ceased to be good Masons, and

''The provisions of this Section shall also apply in respect to a request for
issuance of a sixty (60) year button, a seventy (70) year button, and a
seventy-five (75) year button."

WHEREAS, in such cases, as a condition for re-admission, the Brethren are
required to pay a penalty fee in the form of dues for a predetermined number of
years,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that where a Brother has had a
discontinuance of membership due to suspension for non-payment of dues,
service credit be given to the Brother equivalent to the number of years dues
which he was caused to pay as condition for re-admission into the Lodge, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that a per capita tax, based on the rate in
effect at the time of re-instatement of the Brother, be sent to the Grand Lodge,
and that the Grand Lodge accordingly credit that Brother for years of service
corresponding to the number of years of per capita tax submitted.

RESOLVED FURTHER, that in the third paragraph of Section 2436, immediately following the words "fifty (50) year" there be inserted the following:

Respectfully submitted,

" ... a sixty (60) year button, a seventy (70) year button, ... "

EZRA c. LEVY, PM No. 42

Referred to Committees on Policy, Jurisprudence and on Finance.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 18 would give a "service credit" equivalent to the number of
years that dues were paid as a condition for reinstatement of membership where a
Brother had been suspended for the non-payment of dues, and that these "service
credits" would count toward qualification for a 50-year Veteran's Award.
It is suggested that service time is lost due to the inability of a member to pay
his dues. The C.M.C. in Section 2810 specifically provides that a Lodge may
remit the dues of members who are unable to pay them. Therefore, service time
would not necessarily be lost in the proper situation where the Brother truly was
unable to pay his dues. Dues are considered paid upon their remission and as
such, continuity of membership in good standing is maintained.
Therefore, the argument in support of this Resolution essentially fails. To pass
the Resolution could seriously dilute the esteem in which the 50-year Veteran's
Award is held in that it would permit a situation in which it might be said that it
was purchased.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Finance:
Your Finance Committee considers that any benefit Grand Lodge might gain
fr~m payment of previous per capita assessments does not warrant sacrificing the
prmctple of contmous Masonic service in the award of Veterans' buttons.
We therefore concur with Policy and General Purposes and recommend a
"No" vote.
The ~rand Secretary favorably expressed his concurrence with the report of
the Pohcy and General Purposes Committee.
Not Adopted.

The proponents of Resolution No. 18 seek to amend the California Masonic
Code to provide that where a Brother has had a discontinuance of membership
due to suspension for non-payment of dues due to inability to pay, service credit
be given to the Brother equivalent to the number of years dues which he was
caused to pay as condition for re-admission into the Lodge, and that a per capita

to the Grand Lodge, and that the Grand Lodge credit that Brother for years of

To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the

paragraph thereof, the following:
"provided, further, that where a Brother has had a discontinuance of membership due to suspension for non-payment of dues because of inability to pay,
membership credit shall be given to the Brother equivalent to the number of
past years for which he was caused to pay dues as a condition for restoration
into the Lodge, and provided further, that the per capita tax in effect at the time
of restoration applied to the total dues paid for prior years and for the year in
which restoration occurs shall be paid to the Grand Lodge immediately after
the Brother is restored, with a report to the Grand Lodge showing the years for
which dues were paid in whole or in part, and if said report is made to the
Grand Lodge and such per capita tax is paid, then the Grand Lodge shall
thereupon credit the Brother for membership in good standing for years for
which dues were thus paid in full.''

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In order to protect the innocent (who seldom need protection), current laws
and regulations as administered by several governmental agencies or bureaus
make it difficult to secure detailed consumer information.
Further, if consumer information should be attained without compliance with
all applicable rules and regulations, the entity and/or its agents, who has so
attained the information, may be subject to severe legal repercussions.
So that our Lodges and members thereof may properly investigate candidates
for membership, the Grand Secretary has prepared addenda to the applications
for degrees and affiliation. These addenda, when properly signed by an applicant, grant permission to Lodges and members to conduct thorough investigations
without fear of reprisal from a candidate who because of rejection or for some
other reason, may later become disgruntled.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 2604, C. M. C., reads as follows:
''A person who has pleaded guilty or no lo contendere or has been convicted in
the co.W:ts of a fc!J.ony or of a misdemeanor which is morally wrong in itself, is
not eligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry unless, for the reason that he
did not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of
conviction vacated."
This ~esolution would delete from that section the language, "for the reason
~at he did not commit the offense.'' This would make a very substantial change
m our law. It would not merely clarify a possible misinterpretation.
· A pardon or vacation of a judgment of conviction may be obtained even
though the offense was actually committed. For example, a man who commits a
burglary or even a robbery may be granted probation under certain circumstances. If he successfully completes his probation, even though it may include up
to on~ ~ear in the county jail, he can then take action to vacate the judgment of
conviction, have a plea of Not Guilty entered and the charge dismissed. If he was
convicted and sentenced to prison, the Governor may pardon him, despite the
fact that he has been imprisoned and actually committed the offense.
On the other hand, it is true that mistakes can be made in courts. If a man is
pardoned or his conviction is set aside because he should not have been convicted
because he did not commit the offense, we should not prevent him from applying
for the degrees of Masonry.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

CHANGES TO MASONIC FUNERAL SERVICE

(27)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, recent changes have been made by the Grand Lecturer to the
Masonic Funeral Service; and
WHEREAS, these changes are considered by many Grand Lodge members to
be arbitrary, capricious, and detract from the public image of Masonry by
restricting the movement of the individual conducting the Funeral Service,
namely, during the display of the Masonic Apron, and during the delivery of the
"Evergreen" and "Soft and Safe" portions of our ritual, thereby relegating the
Funeral Service to a mere recitation of words having little meaning to the
uninformed; and
WHEREAS, Section 2690 of the C.M.C. provides that "The Grand Lodge
alone has the power to authorize any changes in the ritual . . . . "
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that any changes to the Masonic
Funeral Service be considered under the purview of Section 2690, and be
handled the same as for changes to our ritualistic work.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that emphasis be placed on the proficiency of
the individual conducting the Funeral Service, rather than make changes to the
Funeral Service that is considered by many to be the ultimate in simplicity and
content, and which reflects the best public image that Masonry in California cari
achieve.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the autonomous authority of the Grand
Lecturer, and/or the Ritual Committee, be subject to the same review as is now
required of the Grand Master in decisions made by him during his term of office,
and that this recent change instituted by the Grand Lecturer be reviewed by the
Grand Lodge at its next Annual Convocation and either approved or rescinded by
vote of the members present.
Respectfully submitted,
HARRY B. CoNWAY, JR., PM No. 396
wALLACE D. MIRACLE, PM No. 396

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and on
Ritual.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 27 proposes "That the autonomous authority of the Grand
Lecturer and/or Ritual Committee be subject to the same review as is now
required of the Grand Master in decisions made by him during his term of office''
and that the recent changes in the Funeral Service "Instituted by the Grand
Lecturer be reviewed by Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication and
either approved or rescinded by vote of the members present."
The highest office that can be bestowed upon a Master Mason in this
Jurisdiction is that of Grand Master, and Section 1052 C.M.C. requires that
every official act, decision or recommendation made by the Grand Master be
":ported at th~ Annual Communication of Grand Lodge for its approval or
disapproval. Smee Grand Lodge requires this of the Grand Master, then should
not Grand Lodge require the same of the Grand Lecturer?
The office of Grand Lecturer in this Jurisdiction is an elective office, although
in many jurisdictions it is an appointive office. The Grand Lecturer is elected by
the Brethren of Grand Lodge, and it follows that his acts, decisions and
recommendations should require the same approval or disapproval of the Brethren as those of the Grand Master, Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary, who
also are elected officers of Grand Lodge.
It is the opinion of~our Committee on Policy and General Purposes that Grand
Lodge never intended to invest the Grand Lecturer or the Committee on Ritual
with the increasing authority which gradually has been assumed. This assumed
authority extends beyond that of any committee or elected officer of Grand
Lodge, including the Grand Master.
The sole responsibility of the Committee on Ritual as custodian of the esoteric
work (Section 1235 C.M.C.) obviously is to maintain conformity to and
uniformity in the work. Nothing tends to destroy the uniformity more quickly
than ~quent changes imposed upon the officers of the Constituent Lodges.
Section 1114- lst C.M.C. states in part: "It shall be the duty of the Grand
Lecturer to require conformity with the adopted ritual and work.''
This brings us to the crucial question. Does the Ritual Committee have the
authority to make changes of the kind contained in the letters of November 1,
1976 and June 1, 1977, ordering changes in the Funeral Service without the
approval of the Grand Lodge?
We have carefully considered our law and our past practice. As a result we
conclude that the action taken is not in accord with either.
We have considered California Masonic Code Sections 2690, 1114 and 1235,
among ?thers. We have also considered past editions of Ross Digest and the
preceedmgs of Grand Lodge for many years, specifically including 1928, 1929,
1946, 1947, 1954 and 1958.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We have carefully considered the possibility of a distinction between ritual and
ceremony , or ritual and floorwork.
.
The history of our ceremonies is that they have been estabbshe d by the Grand
Lodge and changed by the Grand Lodge. Past Grand Lecturers have referred to
our ceremonies as ritual. The California Masonic Code says that only the Grand
Lodge can authorize a change in our ritual. It says nothin~ about ceremonies.
This is no oversight. They have always been regarded as ntual.
As to floorwork, when we consider all the printed footnotes, directions and
instructions by which we must abide as a part of our ritual there appears to be no
question but that floorwork is a part of ritual.
At the 1955 Annual Communication, Elbert W. Davis, Grand Lecturer and the
Committee on Ritual recomme nded and presented to Grand Lodge proposed
changes in the Funeral Service containing 13 numbered footnotes .relating to
instructions for the Master's movements and floorwork ( 1955 Proceedmgs, pages
224-230). The entire Funeral Service including these 13 instructional footnotes
was adopted by Grand Lodge.
.
..
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is convmced by the provision
s
of our law and practices of the Ritual Committee and Grand Lecturer in the past
that:
1. The Ritual referred to in Section 2690 of the California Masonic Code
includes all ceremonies, including the Funeral Service.
2. That any proposed revisions, corrections, or additions to our Ritual,
including all ceremonies, monitors and books of instructions require the
approval of the Grand Lodge.
Brethren, this is your Grand Lodge. You, the Masters, Wardens and Past
Masters are the Grand Lodge of California. You have the right to vote on matters
brought before Grand Lodge, and you are entitled to express your ?pinion by the
exercise of that vote. Unless proposed or recommended changes m the adopted
ritual and work are presented to Grand Lodge for your consideration, you are
being denied that right.
.
.
It is the carefully considered judgment of your Committee on Polley and
General Purposes that this Resolution should be approved.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes unanimously recommends a
"Yes" vote.

Ritual Committee have changed are matters of ceremony . The various changes in
ceremony that have been made by the Ritual Committee have been necessary, in
order that the ritual taught and used by this Grand Jurisdiction is the same
anywhere in this State or the State of Hawaii. These include movements of
Officers in the conferring of the several degrees and the many Grand Lodge
Ceremonies, and in all cases has helped to clarify certain positions and movements of the various Brethren involved, such as the handling of the candidate in
the third degree, the Senior Deacons' moves in the second section of the second
degree, the Masters' movements in the several degrees, the Grand Lodge
Officers' movements in the opening of this great Grand Lodge, and many, many
more.
The California Funeral Service ritual has not been changed; only the modification of movements, which was done primarily for the purpose of preventing some
rather unfortunate incidents which were occuring as a result of the Master
moving about between the podium and the casket. We might also add, at this
point, that this modification of movements, has made a tremendous improvem ent
in the Ceremony. Your Committee on Ritual was not being arbitrary when this
change was made. We had many reasons . We had reports of the individual
conducting the service, to have tripped over flower arrangements, while moving
toward the casket, knocking them down, causing mass confusion and invoking
chuckles and laughter among the mourners in the audience. Now we ask you,
Brethren of this Grand Lodge, is this not a good reason for making this change?
We have had comments from Ministers throughout this Jurisdiction, telling us
that we have an excellent service, but t~e question always arises, "why do you
need to move around so much?" Many churches and chapels in which our service
is conducted, have podiums that make it extremely difficult for the funeral
officiant to trave~e between that podium and the casket. Another reason, and we
think very important, is that when a microphone is needed in a large church or
chapel, or when the audience is required to sit in adjacent rooms or even stand
outside, due to a large attendance, we have several minutes, in our service, in
which the officiant would be away from the microphone, making it impossible
for them to hear. Brethren, the family and friends of the deceased Brother are
entitled to hear every word of our great Funeral Service. Reason? We had many
reasons for making this change in ceremony.
We have opened up a whole new field of members who could not be qualified
to perform our Funeral Service, by not requiring them to revert to their memory
at. a most critical time, while they are away from the podium. There is not now,
with this change, the requireme nt to memorize our service, or any part of it, if a
man is qualified to deliver it with the use of notes or the Funeral Service in front
of him on the podium. There will not now be any reason for the need of
prompting, which has never looked good at a most solemn time. Nervousness on
the part of the officiant in regard to the Funeral Service is only a natural thing that
happens among individuals who are not thoroughly prepared. We have removed
a portion of the reason for this happening.
Your Committee on Ritual was not being capricious when this change was
made, unless you consider over two years of gathering information and many,

RECOMMENDED CHANGE IN FUNERAL SERVICE
(28)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Funeral Service is a literary and spiritual
masterpiece of comfort to the bereaved family, and
.
.
.
WHEREAS, it still fulfills its purpose when the remams are mterred m the
.
ground or entombed in a crypt, and
WHEREAS, during the past twenty years the percentage of cremations has
risen sharply, to almost 20%, and
WHEREAS, the service is concluded in the church or chapel, when followed
by cremation, and
.
WHEREAS, the ashes must, by law, be interred in the ground, placed m a
niche or scattered at sea, and
WHEREAS the Committal "Soft and safe to thee, etc" is not then apropos,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Committal "Soft and ~afe
to thee, etc.," be eliminated when the service is to be followed by crematmn,
and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that immediately following the paragraph
"We extend to the bereaved relatives, etc." that the graveside pra~er ~d
benediction, combined into one prayer or separately, be delivered, which will
conclude the service.

Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes and on Ritual.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 28 seeks to change the Committal portion of the Funeral
Service of the Grand Lodge as presently written in order to remove portions
thereof that are believed not to be appropriate where a Brother is to be cremated.
Also, it seeks to change the graveside prayer and benediction.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has reviewed the Funeral
Service and unanimously reaffirms its position that the purpose of the Service is
purely symbolic and a beautiful tribute to a deceased Brother. We are also
mindful that in some cases the remains of the Brother may not be present during
the Memorial Funeral Service, or may be interred above ground in a crypt, and
we use the same Service.
Therefore, the deletion of the phraseology suggested by the proponents of this
Resolution, in the eyes of your Committee, is unnecessary in view of the
symbolism and might institute an erosion of the true character of the Funeral
Service if approved.
We move the adoption of the Resolution, but recommend a "No" vote.

.

The Committee on Ritual:
The proponents of Resolution No. 28 propose to eliminate the Committal
"Soft and safe to thee" with the simple explanation that it is not apropos when
cremation is to follow. Your Committee on Ritual disagrees. When the Commital
is given we speak not to the mortal remains of our departed Brother but to his
spirit which has entered into "that house not made with hands, eternal in the
heavens." Why, then, should the Commital not be given?
The proponents state that the present Funeral Service is a literary and spiritual
masterpiece of comfort to the bereaved family. If this be true why should it be
changed?
Your Committee on Ritual moves the adoption of the Resolution and recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

INCREASE RELIEF MAXIMUM REFUND TO $100
(30)
To the Mos~ Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code, Section 2902-REFUNDING-limits the amount of money to twenty-five dollars ($25.00) that

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

may be advanced to a Sojourner without first obtaining the permission of the
Sojourner's Lodge; and
WHEREAS, experience has proven that the twenty-five dollars ($25.00)
advance for relief is not a sufficient amount of money in many cases to assist a
Sojourner;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2902 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:

Doll~s. ($25.00) to One Hundred Dollars($100.00) without first obtaining
pemnss10n from the Brother's Lodge, and to require prior authorization for
amounts in excess thereof.
To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2902 be amended to read as follows:

258

"Section 2902 REFUNDING. A Lodge of which a needy Sojourner is a
member shall refund to any other Masonic Lodge or Masonic Service Bureau,
all sums not exceeding one hundred dollars ($100.00) advanced by such other
Lodge or Service Bureau for the relief of such Sojourner; provided, however,
should the Master of the needy Sojourner's Lodge authorize the other Lodge
or Service Bureau to advance sums in excess of one hundred dollars
($100.00), all sums so advanced shall be refunded by such Lodge."
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR R. KIRK, PM No. 403
FRANK D. ROSEN, PM No . 520
WILBUR B. TAYLOR, PM No. 400

JOSEPH L. OUSLEY, PM No. 648
HOWARDS. FISHER, PM No. 620

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and on
Masonic Service Bureaus.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 2902 of the CMC concerns the refunding of relief granted to a needy
member by another Masonic Lodge. Resolution No. 30 would amend this section
to provide for an increase from $25.00 to an amount not to exceed $100.00 in any
one case, which a Lodge shall refund for relief granted by another Lodge or
Masonic Service Bureau. It retains the requirement that anything in excess of
$100.00 must be approved by the needy Brother's Lodge.
It is a sad fact of our economy that the dollar no longer enjoys its former
purchasing power. Today, inflation has substantially reduced the relief obtainable with $25.00; a meal or two, a night's lodging and street car fare for one day,
perhaps.
To increase the maximum amount permitted to $100.00 in any one case,
hardly keeps pace with inflation as we know it today. The purpose of the Section,
to provide fast relief for a needy Brother, is commendable, and keeping pace
with the cost is prudent. .
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
The proponents of Resolution No. 30 seek to amend the California Masonic
Code to increase the amount of money that may be advanced to a needy Brother
by another Lodge or Masonic Service Bureau in any one case from Twenty-Five

259

"REFUNDING. A Lodge of which a needy Brother is a member shall refund
to any other Masonic Lodge or Masonic Service Bureau, all sums not
exceeding One Hundred Dollars ($100.00) advanced in any one case by such
other Lodge or Service Bureau for the relief of said Brother; provided,
however, that should the Master of the needy Brother's Lodge authorize the
other Lodge or Service Bureau to advance sums in excess of One Hundred
Dollars ($100.00) in any one case, all sums so advanced shall be refunded by
such Lodge."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus:
Resolution No. 30 seeks to amend our California Masonic Code to provide for
an increase in the amount of money that may be advanced to a needy Brother
from $25.00 to $100.00 without first obtaining approval from the needy
·
Brother's home Lodge.
Your Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus has discussed the $25 .00 limit
with. the Officers and the Executive Secretaries of the nineteen (19) Masonic
Service Bureaus in this Grand Jurisdiction and they all agree that this limit is not
sufficient amount of money to be advanced for temporary relief in many cases.
Also, because t>f the time difference between the East Coast and California in
many cases it is not always possible to secure a telephone approval from tlte
needy Brother's Lodge for an advance of funds.
The then Grand Master William H. Price approved an increase from $25.00 to
$!00.00 on Marc~ 30, 1973 for the Service Bureaus. He reported this increase in
his message to this Grand Lodge in October, 1973. However, the new California
Masonic Code still carries the limit of $25.00.
The sum of $25.00 has been the monetary limit since 1926 and in view of the
inflatio_n that has <><_:curred during the past fifty years and the experience of our
Executive Secretaries of our Service Bureaus, your Committee on Masonic
Service Bureaus concurs that the amount of money should be increased to
$100.00.
We move the adoption of Resolution No. 30 and recommend a "Yes" vote.
Adopted 5/6 vote.

Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes,
Finance, and Temple Properties.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 33 seeks to create a Building Assistance Fund to be funded by
the members of all of our Constituent Lodges through assessments and administered through Grand Lodge. The money in the fund would be available to Lodges
and Lodge Temple Associations for remodeling of existing Masonic Temples or
construction of new Masonic Temples.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes there are several
policy reasons dictating against the passage of this Resolution .

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

Initially, Grand Lodge is not in the banking business, and to start at this late
date would institute a bad precedent. Where would it stop? The next fund might
be that which could be used by an applicant for the degrees of Masonry for his
initiation fee if he were not financially able. There might be a request to start a
fund to be used for Lodge furnishings.
Further, your Committee questions how such a Building Assistance Fund
could be equitably divided and it would be extremely difficult to administer.
Additionally, from a practical standpoint, the propriety of such a Fund is
questionable. A Masonic Temple is primarily a single purpose building. In the
event of foreclosure the sale of such a building is difficult if not impossible. Who
would then suffer the loss but Grand Lodge?
Finally, the funding of the Building Assistance Fund would be still another
assessment burden to be incurred by all the members of Lodges in California and
Hawaii, with the ultimate benefit to only a relative few.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
The proponents of Resolution No. 33 seek to amend the California Masonic
Code to create a Building Assistance Fund by providing for a Five Dollar ($5.00)
assessment against each Master Mason on the rolls of each Lodge as of January
l, 1978 and Two Dollars ($2.00) in the years 1979 to 1988, inclusive, to provide
financial assistance to remodel existing Masonic Temples or for construction of
new Masonic Temples within the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge.
To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED , th·at Section 1704 of the California Masonic Code be amended
by adding a new subsection "4th" as follows:
"4th. For each member borne upon its rolls as of January 1, 1978, the sum of
Five Dollars ($5.00), and for each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of
January 1, in the years 1979 to 1988, both inclusive, the sum of Two Dollars
($2.00) in each of said years. Said sums shall be placed in the Building
Assistance Fund of Grand Lodge. Said sums shall be assessed by the Lodge
against each member of a Lodge other than plural members thereof and those
whose dues have been remitted."
RESOLVED FURTHER, that there be added to the California Masonic Code
Sections 1550, 1552, 1554 and 1556 as follows:
"Section 1550. BUILDING ASSISTANCE FUND. There is hereby created
a Building Assistance Fund to consist of the funds received by Grand Lodge
pursuant to Section 1704, sub-paragraph 4th of this Code, which funds shall be
placed in the custody of the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge to be held by
him as such, and to be by him accounted for and disbursed pursuant to the
provisions of Section 1102."
"Section 1552. OBJECTIVE AND LOANS. The purpose of said Fund is to
assist in remodeling existing Masonic Temples, or constructing new Masonic

264

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Temples, by loaning the Fund to them at nominal interest rates and repayable
on terms established as hereinafter set forth, which loans shall be evidenced by
Promissory Notes secured or unsecured as determined by the Committee. The
income from loans shall be added to the Fund."
"Section 1554. COMMITTEE. The Grand Master shall appoint a Committee on Building Assistance to consist of three (3) members who shall, with the
approval of the Grand Master, establish rules and regulations for the lending of
the funds, including terms and rates of interest, the type and amount of
security for the notes, if any, and who shall pass upon all applications of
Lodges and Lodge Temple Associations for loans. The Grand Master shall
name the Chairman of the Committee. The members of the Committee shall be
reimbursed from the Fund for their necessary expenses incurred in the
performance of their duties pursuant to Section 1150 of this Code.''
"Section 1556. DISBURSEMENT OF FUNDS. The Grand Treasurer shall
disburse the Fund to the Grand Secretary to be paid to such Lodges or Lodge
Temple Associations as directed by the Committee pursuant to Section 1108,
and shall hold all notes, security documents and evidences of the indebtedness
in connection with any loans pursuant to Section 1102."
RESOLVED FURTHER, that Section 1202 be amended by adding at the end
of the first sentence the following:
", and on Building Assistance to consist of three members."
RESOLVED FURTHER, that Section 2808 be amended by adding at the end
thereof the following:
"except as provided in Section 1704."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of the
Resolution.

The Committee on Finance:
Resolution No. 33 is presented on the premise that a financial need exists with
certain individual Lodges. It proposes the establishment of a loan fund requiring
a ten-year assessment to each and every member of this Jurisdiction. Your
Committee feels this fund is not needed for the following reasons:
1. The sudden impact of the $7.00 first year assessment, over and above the
normal Grand Lodge per capita assessment of $3. 75 (nearly a 200% increase)
would be disturbing, if not prohibitive, to many individual Masons. The ten-year
proposal would undoubtedly cause some demits and loss of membership.
2. Grand Lodge should nor attempt to compete with established lending
agencies. Administrative costs such as appraisal, documentation, accounting and
collections, together with the Solomon-type expertise necessary for granting of
loans, are significant. More importantly, the possibility of placing our non-profit
status in jeopardy is a real threat.
3. By removing the initiative of the individual Lodge to solve its own
problems, a Lodge is encouraged to "go to Uncle Sam for the dough" .
4. If the proponents had taken the time to understand the workings of Grand
Lodge Committees and had consulted both the Lodge Resources Development

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

265

Committee and the Temple Properties Committee, this Resolution may never
have been presented.
Your Committee on Finance strongly recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Temple Properties:
Resolution No . 33 would assess all Master Masons for eleven years to create a
Building Assistance Fund. The funds would be deposited with the Grand
Treasurer and administered by a three-man committee. The committee would be
appointed by the Grand Master and it would use the funds by loaning the same to
assist Lodges and Temple Associations in remodeling and new construction. The
loans would be at nominal interest rates and could be secured or unsecured.
Historically Lodges have raised funds for building purposes from gifts, fund
raising activities and commercial borrowing.
If we assume a membership of 215,000 members the assessment would raise
$5,375,000.
Since we are a Fraternity each of our members should be treated alike. Our
present Temples vary in value from possibly thirty thousand dollars to in excess
of three or four million dollars so it can be expected that requests for funds would
be equally disparate.
If requests for funds were approved as received it is likely that the fund would
be exhausted within a year or two. Since the pay-off on a real estate loan might
take ten or more years, the money in the fund would not revolve rapidly and there
would be long dry periods.
The committee members should be experienced bankers or lending institution
officers to satisfy themselves of the value of the security to be received and the
ability of the borrowers to repay. Undoubtedly the committee would need the
assistance of one ot more lawyers and a staff of persons to keep the records and
oversee the loans. The time and expense to the fund for administration is difficult
to calculate but would be substantial.
Undoubtedly some loans would default and foreclosure proceedings would be
necessary to protect the interests of the contributors. The hard feelings engendered by slow payment, delinquent accounts and foreclosures would be incalcuable.
At least one nationwide church has a program for assisting local congregations
obtain meeting places. These funds, however, were created in the main by gifts
from the estates of deceased members, are not reported to the public nor even the
general membership, pay no income taxes and involve rather fluid local memberships. Further, in the event of a dissolution of the local body the assets become
the property of the governing organization.
The overriding problem involves the allocation of funds among the prospective
borrowers. Should a Lodge with 500 members and several hundred thousand
dollars in assets be permitted to borrow thirty thousand dollars to install air
conditioning as opposed to a Lodge of seventy members, assets of five or ten
thousand dollars that desires to borrow thirty thousand dollars which, with
donated labor and materials, would permit them to build a Temple? The
variations on this theme are infinite.

would prevail.

School; Joseph L. Grable, Master of Rim of the World Lodge No. 711, using the

Water Complex; and Charles F. Gilb, Master of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42,

Justice Building; at the 75th Anniversary Celebration of San Bernardino Lodge
No. 348 and at the Annual Family Barbecue of Poinsettia Lodge No. 633.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
In compliance with our Code, the Grand Treasurer has presented to this
Communication audited financial statements for the fiscal year ended June 30,
1977.
Your Committee on Finance is concerned not only with establishing a budget
for Grand Lodge operations, expenses and activities, but also with overseeing
this budget and the overall financial condition of Grand Lodge. The budgeting
task is comparatively easy; much of our concern is in the area of expense control.
Unfortunately not all Brethren charged with spending Grand Lodge funds seem
to share our great concern in controlling expenses. Our report will therefore
emphasize the control of expenses.
For the second consecutive year your Committee will recommend a deficit
budget, the highest budget in Grand Lodge history. Your Committee has strong
feelings that belt tightening in certain areas can be improved upon.
The following tabulation shows a comparison of 1977 expenditures in four
major e;Kpense categories with those same items five years ago.

The increase in salaries, based on comparable job classifications in the San
Francisco area, appears to be reasonable.
The Grand Master and Grand Lodge Officers' Travel expense is an area that
has increased cons\derably; and we feel that improvement can be made.
We are all aware of the increased cost of insurance as we are unable to control
a large portion of this expenditure.
We commend the Grand Lodge Chairmen and their Committees for their
diligent effort in keeping their expenses within a reasonable area.of increase.
Your Committee on Finance wholeheartedly concurs with the Grand
Treasurer's comment "To the end that better controls be provided in our
financial affairs, your Grand Treasurer recommends that no funds in excess of
the budgeted amounts authorized by this Grand Lodge, be paid out, unless
approved by the Committee on Finance and/or authorized by the Grand Master.''
Hopefully this suggestion can be implemented during the present fiscal year.
The report of our Grand Treasurer contains the usual reference to supplemental
appropriations covering those items which exceeded the budget, this year
amounting to $61,525, duly approved by the Grand Master. We recommend your
approval of this action.
We extend to our Grand Treasurer appreciation for his usual factual report; we
are happy to move its approval.
Our Masonic Homes Trustees have again requested a $1.00 per capita. We
concur with this request and will include this item in our closing motion.
Your Committee on Finance at this time suggests to the Homes Trustees that
they consider a substantial reduction in this requested allocation a year hence.

Even with the increased per capita allocation of $.50 for our fine California
Freemason Magazine, the continual increases in publishing costs have resulted in
a budgeted deficit this year of $8,600.00. Evidently we must look to future
increases in the per capita to maintain a balanced budget.
In cases where Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors, Committeemen, and Staff
must use their private automobiles on Grand Lodge business, we recommend
continuance of the milage allowance reimbursement of $.13 per mile from the
close of this Annual Communication until the corresponding date in 1978. It
should be noted that this reimbursement rate has no connection with the mileage
allowance to Lodge Representatives attending Grand Lodge Communications.
The usual and continuous assistance of the Grand Secretary and his Staff, as
well as the Elective Line, the Committies and Boards of Grand Lodge is greatly
appreciated.
Such matters in the Grand Master's Message and in the several Resolutions
and Reports which have been approved by this Grand Lodge and now require
funds have been provided for in the proposed budget.

FURNITURE, EQUIPMENT AND IMPROVEMENTS

We have examined the statement of aasets, liabilities and fund balance
arising from cash transactions of The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California, a nonprofit, unincorporated, fraternal
organization, as of June 30, 1977 and 1976, and the related statement of revenues
and expensea for the years then ended, Our examination was made in accordance with
generally accepted auditing standards, and accordingly included such tests of the
accounting records and auch other auditing procedures aa ve considered necessary in

LIABILITIES:

statements on the basis of cash receipts and disburaementa; consequently, certain
revenue and related aasets are recognized when received rather than when earned and

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Basis of Ace ounting:
The financial statements are presented on a modified cash
basis of accounting. Certain revenue and related assets are recognized
when received rather than vhen earned, and certain expenses are recognized
when paid rather than vhen incurred.
Investments:

Investments in securities purchased are carried at cost and

oecuritie• re.:eived by gift or bequest are carried at approximate market
value on the date received. Gains and losaea are recorded vhen investments are sold. Investments are not written down to market unless a
permanent impairment in the value of such investments is considered to
have occurred.
Furniture, Equipment and Improvements:
Additions and betterments to property are capitalized at
coat and are not depreciated. Expenditures which represent maintenance
and repairs are charged to expense. The property accounts are relieved
of cost upon dispo1ition.

We have examined the statement of assets, liabilities and fund
balances arising from cash transactions of Masonic Homes of California, a
nonprofit corporation, including the permanent endowment, property and
restricted trust funds, as of June 30, 1977 and 1976, and the related statements of revenues and expenses and changes in fund balances for the years

then ended. Our examination was made in accordance with generally accepted
auditing standards, and accordingly included such tests of the accounting
records and such other auditing procedures as we considered necessary in

the circ1.DDStances.

•As described in Note 1, the policy of Masonic Homes of California
is to prepare its financial statements on the modified cash basis of accounting; consequently, certain revenue and related assets are recognized when
received rather than when earned, and certain expenses are recognized when
paid rather than when incurred. Accordingly, we are required to report that
this policy does not present the financial position and results of operations
in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles.
In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above
present fairly the assets, liabilities and fund balances arising from the
cash transactions of the Masonic Homes of California at June 30, 1977 and
1976, and its revenues collected and expenses paid and changes in fund
balances for the years then ended, on the basis of accounting described in
Note 1, applied in a manner consistent with the preceding year.

NOTE 1:

I ~I

OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Basis of Accounti!!&:

S~RY

The financial statements are stated on a modified cash basis of
accounting. Ganarally, revenue and related assets are recognized when
received rather than when earned, and expenses are recogniz"d when paid
rather than when incurred. Payroll costs are an exception and are
recorded when incurred.

I ;1

Investments:

~I

Investments in aecurities purchased are carried at cost and
securities received by gift or bequeat are carried at approximate
market value '>n the date received. Gains and losaes are recorded when
investments ar'! sold. Investments are not written down to market
unleu a permanent impairment in the val-le of such investments is
considered to have occurred.
Other Assets:
Other assets consist of life insurance policies, real estate,
and mineral right• assigned or bequeathed to the Masonic Homes. These
asseta are recorded at the nominal value of $1 each for accountability.
Payments by the Masonic Homes of obligation• of the assignors secured
by these assets are added to the nominal value, with the exception of
life insurance premiuma which are charged to expense when paid,
Property:

.
I.
J

Additions and betterments to property are capitalized at cost
and are not depreciated. Expenditures which repreaent maintenance and
repairs are charged to expense. The property accounts are relieved of
cost upon disposition •
Reserves for Special Purposes:
The trustees have established various special reserves to
which are added gifts and bequests and other amounts which generally are
used at the direction of the trustees for purposes other than direct
operating expenses. '11le assets represented by these reserves are included
in the assets of the General Fund.
Federai and State Income Taxes:
The Masonic Homes of California is a charitable organization
exempt from federal and state income taxes.

John and Lena Luckenbach Fund:
The principal of this fund, restricted by the terms of the
wil 1 of the donor, is to be kept intact and the income used only for
the benefit of the care of orphans or the aged in Masonic Home• of
Southern California.
George F. and Laura E. Brigham Scholarship Fund:
The principal of this fund is held as a scholarship Fund for
the benefit of the Covina Home residents, of which $25,000 may be
loaned for this purpoae. Income of this fund is restricted and may be
used only for providing acholarahips.
Walter W. and Maude S. Schultz Scholarship Fund:
The income from this fund is restricted and may be used only
to provide financial assistance to needy children for educational
purposes.

Hildred R. Brown and Leroy G. Brown Memorial Fund:
Principal and income from this fund are to be used for making
loans for educational purposes to any children that the Board of Trustees
deem Worthy.
Frederick E. and Frieda E. Sommers Trust:
Thia fund is to be used exclusively for the education of
full orphan children.
George H. and Florence G. Perine Endowment Fund:
The principal of thia fund, subject to the provision included
in the will of the donor shall be kept intact and only the income
therefrom shall be used for the benefit of the Decoto Home.
Harriet c. Wadleigh Endowment Annuity Fund:
This fund, in the original amount of $30,000 ia subject to
a contract with the donor providing for the payments of certain life
annuities out of the principal and income thereof. Under the terms of
the contract, principal of the fund expended in payment of the annuities
ia to be later restored out of income when the annuities no longer
ab a orb the entire income. After restoration of the principal to the
original sum of $30,000, the income from the fund is to be used for
the benefit of the residents of the Covina Home.

balances arising from cash transactions of California Masonic Foundation, a

procedures as we considered necessary in the circumatancea.

disbursements; consequently, certain revenue and related assets are recognized
when received rather than when earned, and certain expenses are recognized
when paid rather than when incurred, Accordingly, we are required to report
that this policy does not present the financial position and results of
operations in confoxmity with generally accepted accounting principles.
'Ibe excess of carrying value over market value of General Fund
common stocks is attributable to one stock iaveatment, as explained in Note 2

permaneo.t or temporary.

ORGANIZATION:
The Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund was organized on October 15,
1974 and ia a charitable remainder trust to which donors contribute
irrevocable remainder interests in property while retaining an income
interest for life for one or more beneficiaries. The donors are entitled
to a tax deduction equivalant to the present value of the remainder
interest in the property contributed.

The property transferred by such donor is held in trust by the
Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund and 1a collingled with and invested and reinvested with other properties transferred
to the Fund. All income of the Fund is distributed quarterly to the
beneficiaries, baaed on their proportionate share of the Pool. Upon the
death of each donor's last income beneficiary, the remainder interest is
distributed to Masonic Homes of California, a charitable corporation.
